claims.statement: Together with Toyoukehime this kami is called one of the yafunegami ("kami of houses") and is still worshiped today at roof-raising ceremonies and blessings of new houses.
claims.statement_id: Bersama Toyoukehime, kami ini disebut salah satu yafunegami ("kami rumah") dan hingga kini dipuja pada upacara pemasangan atap dan pemberkatan rumah baru.
claims.quote: Together with Toyoukehime, this kami is referred to as one of the yafunegami ("kami of houses"), and continues to be worshiped today on the occasion of roof raising ceremonies and the blessing of new houses.

claims.statement: It is possible that Kukunochi was originally a tama (spirit) dwelling in trees.
claims.statement_id: Mungkin Kukunochi pada mulanya adalah tama (roh) yang bersemayam di pohon.
claims.quote: It is possible Kukunochi was originally a tama that dwelled in trees.

claims.statement: Many versions state he was born from Izanami and Izanagi, while others state he is the son of Shinatsuhiko.
claims.statement_id: Banyak versi menyatakan ia lahir dari Izanami dan Izanagi, sedangkan versi lain menyatakan ia putra Shinatsuhiko.
claims.quote: Many versions state he was born from Izanami and Izanagi, while others state he is the son of Shinatsuhiko.

claims.statement: He is the brother of Ōyamatsumi, Shimatsuhiko, and Watatsumi.
claims.statement_id: Ia adalah saudara Ōyamatsumi, Shimatsuhiko, dan Watatsumi.
claims.quote: He is the brother of Ōyamatsumi, Shimatsuhiko, and Watatsumi.

claims.statement: Kuraokami is a Japanese dragon deity associated with rain and snow.
claims.statement_id: Kuraokami adalah dewa naga Jepang yang berkaitan dengan hujan dan salju.
claims.quote: Okami (淤加美神, Okami-no-kami) in the Kojiki, or in the Nihon Shoki: Kuraokami (闇龗) or Okami (龗), is a legendary Japanese dragon and Shinto deity of rain and snow.

claims.statement: The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki use different written forms of the name.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki dan Nihon Shoki memakai bentuk tulisan nama yang berbeda.
claims.quote: Okami (淤加美神, Okami-no-kami) in the Kojiki, or in the Nihon Shoki: Kuraokami (闇龗) or Okami (龗), is a legendary Japanese dragon and Shinto deity of rain and snow.

claims.statement: One birth story follows Izanagi’s killing of the fire deity Kagutsuchi.
claims.statement_id: Salah satu kisah kelahirannya mengikuti pembunuhan dewa api Kagutsuchi oleh Izanagi.
claims.quote: After Izanami died from burns during the childbirth of the fire deity Kagu-tsuchi, Izanagi was enraged and killed his son.

claims.statement: Different versions trace Kuraokami to Kagutsuchi’s blood or body.
claims.statement_id: Berbagai versi menghubungkan Kuraokami dengan darah atau tubuh Kagutsuchi.
claims.quote: Kagutsuchi's blood or body, according to differing versions of the legend, created several other deities, including Kuraokami.

claims.statement: The first element of the name is associated with darkness.
claims.statement_id: Unsur pertama namanya dikaitkan dengan kegelapan.
claims.quote: The name Kuraokami combines kura 闇 "dark; darkness; closed" and okami 龗 "dragon tutelary of water".

claims.statement: The second element refers to a dragon linked with water.
claims.statement_id: Unsur kedua menunjuk naga yang berkaitan dengan air.
claims.quote: The name Kuraokami combines kura 闇 "dark; darkness; closed" and okami 龗 "dragon tutelary of water".

claims.statement: The Kojiki version traces Kuraokami to blood dripping through Izanaki’s fingers.
claims.statement_id: Versi Kojiki menghubungkan Kuraokami dengan darah yang menetes di antara jari Izanaki.
claims.quote: Then, the blood pooling on the hilt of Izanaki’s sword oozed from between his fingers. The deity that thereupon came into existence was named Kura okami no kami 闇淤加美 神. Next [appeared] Kura mitsuha no kami 闇御津羽神 (8).

claims.statement: The morpheme kura means a valley or a ravine, and okami is a deity who governs the waters.
claims.statement_id: Unsur kura berarti lembah atau jurang, sedangkan okami adalah dewa yang menguasai air.
claims.quote: The morpheme kura means a valley or a ravine; okami is a deity who governs the waters.

claims.statement: In the Nihon Shoki, the deity comes into being from blood dripping from the sword’s head together with Kura-yamatsumi and Kura-mitsuha, written 闇龗, with a reading note 於箇美 (okami) attached to the character 龗.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Nihon Shoki, dewa ini lahir dari darah yang menetes dari kepala pedang bersama Kura-yamatsumi dan Kura-mitsuha, ditulis 闇龗 dengan catatan bacaan 於箇美 (okami) pada aksara 龗.
claims.quote: 書紀では剣の頭から滴る血から闇山祇（くらやまつみ）・闇罔象（くらみつは）と共に成り、「闇龗」と書いて、「龗」字に「於箇美（オカミ）」の訓注がある。

claims.statement: The Kojiki deity-name database notes that the Bungo no kuni Fudoki writes the word as 蛇龗 and reads it okami, and calls it a dragon-serpent deity living in springs.
claims.statement_id: Basis data nama dewa Kojiki mencatat bahwa Bungo no kuni Fudoki menulis kata ini sebagai 蛇龗 dan membacanya okami, serta menyebutnya dewa naga-ular yang berdiam di mata air.
claims.quote: 『豊後国風土記』直入郡・球覃郷条では「蛇龗」と書いてオカミと読んでおり、泉に棲む竜蛇神である。

claims.statement: The Kojiki deity-name database reads Man’yōshū poem 2:104, which mentions the okami of the poet’s hill in a poem about snowfall, as showing that it was a water deity in charge of rain and snow.
claims.statement_id: Basis data nama dewa Kojiki membaca puisi Man’yōshū 2:104, yang menyebut okami di bukit sang penyair dalam puisi tentang salju, sebagai bukti bahwa ia dewa air yang menguasai hujan dan salju.
claims.quote: また、『万葉集』（2・104）に「我が岡の龗に言ひて降らしめし雪の摧けしそこに散りけむ」とあり、水の神として雨や雪を掌ったことがわかる。

claims.statement: Menreiki is a mask-associated being in Japanese folklore.
claims.statement_id: Menreiki adalah makhluk yang berkaitan dengan topeng dalam cerita rakyat Jepang.
claims.quote: Menreiki (面霊気) is a type of monster in Japanese folklore, composed of Gigaku masks.

claims.statement: Its form is made from gigaku masks.
claims.statement_id: Wujudnya tersusun dari topeng gigaku.
claims.quote: Menreiki (面霊気) is a type of monster in Japanese folklore, composed of Gigaku masks.

claims.statement: It appears in the 1781 Gazu Hyakki Tsurezure Bukuro.
claims.statement_id: Ia muncul dalam Gazu Hyakki Tsurezure Bukuro yang terbit pada 1781.
claims.quote: It is listed within the 1781 compendium of Japanese supernatural entities, entitled Gazu Hyakki Tsurezure Bukuro.

claims.statement: One origin account links its masks with Prince Shotoku and Hata no Kawakatsu.
claims.statement_id: Satu kisah asal-usul menghubungkan topengnya dengan Pangeran Shotoku dan Hata no Kawakatsu.
claims.quote: It is mentioned in folklore that during the time of Prince Shotoku, the prince created various Gigaku masks which were used by Hata no Kawakatsu, and that the Menreiki is based on those masks.

claims.statement: Menreiki (めんれいき) is a mask yokai recorded in the yokai picture collection 『百器徒然袋』 by Toriyama Sekien (鳥山石燕).
claims.statement_id: Menreiki (めんれいき) adalah yokai berwujud topeng yang tercatat dalam kumpulan lukisan yokai 『百器徒然袋』 karya Toriyama Sekien (鳥山石燕).
claims.quote: 面霊気（めんれいき）は、鳥山石燕による妖怪画集『百器徒然袋』にある日本の妖怪の一つで、面の妖怪。

claims.statement: Sekien's explanatory text says that in the time of 聖徳太子, 秦の川勝 made many masks, and the lifelike masks may be 川勝's work.
claims.statement_id: Teks penjelasan 石燕 menyebut bahwa pada masa 聖徳太子, 秦の川勝 membuat banyak topeng, dan topeng yang tampak seolah hidup itu mungkin hasil karya 川勝.
claims.quote: 石燕による解説文には「聖徳太子の時、秦の川勝あまたの仮面を製せしよし。かく生けるがごとくなるは、川勝のたくめる仮面にやあらんと、夢心におもひぬ。」とある。

claims.statement: 泰河勝 (はたのかわかつ) was a figure of the Asuka period said by legend to be founder of 申楽, the performing art that became the root of Noh and Kyōgen; 石燕 says the masks made by 秦河勝 may be the 面霊気.
claims.statement_id: 泰河勝 (はたのかわかつ) adalah tokoh zaman Asuka yang menurut legenda adalah pendiri 申楽, seni pertunjukan cikal bakal Noh dan Kyōgen; 石燕 menyatakan topeng karya 秦河勝 itulah mungkin 面霊気.
claims.quote: 泰河勝（はたのかわかつ）は飛鳥時代の人物で、能・狂言の原型となった芸能・「申楽」の始祖であるという伝説を持つ。そのような、面を使う芸能とゆかりのある秦河勝の作った面がこの「面霊気」であろうかと石燕は述べている。

claims.statement: There is a legend that 聖徳太子 had 秦河勝 make 66 masks for 66 pieces of 神楽 honoring the gods, which became the origin of 申楽 (猿楽); 石燕 is thought to have written the explanation of 面霊気, his invented mask yokai of Noh and Kyōgen, from this legend.
claims.statement_id: Ada legenda bahwa 聖徳太子 menyuruh 秦河勝 membuat 66 topeng untuk 66 nomor 神楽 yang memuliakan para dewa, dan itu menjadi asal 申楽 (猿楽); 石燕 dianggap menulis penjelasan 面霊気, yokai topeng Noh dan Kyōgen ciptaannya, berdasarkan legenda ini.
claims.quote: 神々をまつる六十六番の神楽に使うため、聖徳太子が秦河勝に六十六の面を作らせたことが、後の申楽（猿楽）の元祖となったという伝説があり、この伝説を素材として、石燕は能・狂言の面の妖怪として創作した面霊気の解説文を執筆したと考えられている。

claims.statement: Explanations from the Shōwa and Heisei periods describe it as an aged mask transformed, moving at night, a tsukumogami (付喪神, a yokai from a changed object) from a fine mask grown old and inhabited by a soul, asking its owner to treat it with care.
claims.statement_id: Penjelasan sejak era Shōwa dan Heisei menyebutnya topeng tua yang menjelma, bergerak pada malam hari, tsukumogami (付喪神, yokai dari benda yang berubah) dari topeng berkualitas tinggi yang telah tua dan dihuni jiwa, dan meminta pemiliknya merawatnya dengan baik.
claims.quote: 古くなった面の化けたもので夜になると動き出す、優れた作品の面が古くなって魂を宿した付喪神（器物が変化した妖怪）であり、持ち主に対して大切に扱ってくれるよう頼むなどの解説がある。

claims.statement: Mizuchi is a Japanese dragon or serpent-like being linked with water.
claims.statement_id: Mizuchi adalah naga atau makhluk mirip ular Jepang yang berkaitan dengan air.
claims.quote: The Mizuchi (大虬, 蛟龍, 蛟, 美都知) is a type of Japanese dragon or legendary serpent-like creature, either found in an aquatic habitat or otherwise connected to water.

claims.statement: Some commentators interpret it as a water deity.
claims.statement_id: Sebagian pengulas menafsirkannya sebagai dewa air.
claims.quote: Some commentators perceived it to have been a water deity.

claims.statement: The name appears in the Nihon Shoki and a Man’yōshū poem.
claims.statement_id: Namanya muncul dalam Nihon Shoki dan sebuah puisi Man’yōshū.
claims.quote: It is described in the Nihon Shoki and one Man'yōshū poem.

claims.statement: One analysis divides its old pronunciation into elements for water, possession and spirit.
claims.statement_id: Satu analisis membagi pelafalan lamanya menjadi unsur air, kepunyaan, dan roh.
claims.quote: In olden times pronounced mi-tsu-chi, the word can be broken down to mi "water" + tsu a particle meaning "of" + chi "spirit".

claims.statement: The ancient chronicle Nihongi contains references to mizuchi: in central Kibi Province, at a fork of the Kawashima River (川嶋河, old name of the Takahashi River in Okayama Prefecture), a great water serpent or dragon (大虬) dwelt and spewed venom that poisoned and killed many passersby.
claims.statement_id: Kronik kuno Nihongi memuat rujukan tentang mizuchi: di Provinsi Kibi bagian tengah, di percabangan Sungai Kawashima (川嶋河, nama lama Sungai Takahashi di Prefektur Okayama), seekor ular atau naga air besar (大虬) bermukim dan menyemburkan racun yang membunuh banyak orang yang lewat.
claims.quote: The ancient chronicle Nihongi contains references to mizuchi. ... in central Kibi Province, at a fork on Kawashima River (川嶋河, old name of Takahashi River in Okayama Prefecture), a great water serpent or dragon (大虬) dwelt and would breathe or spew out its venom, poisoning and killing many passersby.

claims.statement: The man approached the river pool, cast three floating calabashes and challenged the beast to sink them, threatening to kill it if it failed; the beast turned into a deer, failed to sink them, and was slain.
claims.statement_id: Sang pria mendekati kolam sungai, melempar tiga labu yang mengapung, dan menantang makhluk itu menenggelamkannya dengan ancaman akan membunuhnya jika gagal; makhluk itu berubah menjadi rusa dan gagal menenggelamkannya, lalu dibunuh.
claims.quote: He approached the pool of the river, cast three calabashes which floated to the surface of the water and challenged the beast to make these gourds sink, threatening to slay it should it fail. The beast transformed into a deer and tried unsuccessfully to sink them, whereby the man slew the monster.

claims.statement: Kunio Yanagita emphasized that although a character like 虬 may suggest a snake-like being, the mizuchi signifies a "water spirit".
claims.statement_id: Kunio Yanagita menekankan bahwa meski aksara seperti 虬 mungkin mengesankan makhluk mirip ular, mizuchi menandakan "roh air".
claims.quote: Kunio Yanagita also emphasized that while the use of character like 虬 may suggest a snake-like being, it should be stressed that the mizuchi signifies a "water spirit".

claims.statement: Minakata also conjectured that in some regions the mizuchi eventually came to be regarded as creatures of the kappa kind.
claims.statement_id: Minakata juga menduga bahwa di sebagian daerah mizuchi akhirnya dianggap makhluk sejenis kappa.
claims.quote: Minakata also conjectured that in some parts of the country, mizuchi eventually came to be regarded as creatures of the kappa kind.

claims.statement: This mizuchi was exterminated by a man named Agatamori (県守), ancestor of the Kasa-no-omi (笠臣) clan.
claims.statement_id: Mizuchi itu dibunuh oleh seorang pria bernama Agatamori (県守), leluhur klan Kasa-no-omi (笠臣).
claims.quote: This mizuchi was exterminated by a man named Agatamori (県守), ancestor of the Kasa-no-omi (笠臣) clan.

claims.statement: According to the Japanese article, 蛟 (みずち; old reading 「みつち」) is a kind of dragon, legendary serpent or water deity regarded as connected with water in Japanese myth and legend.
claims.statement_id: Menurut artikel bahasa Jepang, 蛟 (みずち; bacaan lama 「みつち」) adalah jenis naga, ular legendaris, atau dewa air yang dianggap berkaitan dengan air dalam mitos dan legenda Jepang.
claims.quote: 蛟（みずち；古訓は「みつち」）は、日本の神話・伝説で水と関係があるとみなされる竜類か伝説上の蛇類または水神。

claims.statement: 南方熊楠 wrote that in Japan too the various snakes living by the water and feared by people seem to have been called ミヅチ in the sense of "master of the water".
claims.statement_id: 南方熊楠 menulis bahwa di Jepang pun berbagai ular yang tinggal di tepi air dan ditakuti orang tampaknya disebut ミヅチ dengan arti "penguasa air".
claims.quote: 南方熊楠は、『十二支考・蛇』の冒頭で、「わが邦でも水辺に住んで人に怖れらるる諸蛇を水の主というほどの意〔こころ〕でミヅチと呼んだらしい」としている。

claims.statement: 『和名抄』 has entries for 「虬龍」, 「螭龍」 and 「蛟」; of these 「蛟」 is given the Japanese name 「美豆知」 and noted as corresponding to 「大虬」 in the 日本書紀.
claims.statement_id: 『和名抄』 memuat entri 「虬龍」, 「螭龍」, dan 「蛟」; di antaranya 「蛟」 diberi nama Jepang 「美豆知」 dan dicatat setara dengan 「大虬」 dalam 日本書紀.
claims.quote: 『和名抄』は、「虬龍」、「螭龍」、「蛟」のいずれの項もあるが、このうち「蛟（こう）」を和名の「美豆知」とし、日本書紀の「大虬（みづち）」に相当すると注釈されている。

claims.statement: In the anime film Spirited Away, the character Haku looks like a Mizuchi and is a river spirit.
claims.statement_id: Dalam anime Spirited Away, tokoh Haku tampak seperti Mizuchi dan merupakan roh sungai.
claims.quote: Spirited Away (anime, movie) – the character Haku looks like a Mizuchi and he is a river spirit.

claims.statement: Mizuhanome is a divinity of water in Japanese mythology.
claims.statement_id: Mizuhanome adalah dewi air dalam mitologi Jepang.
claims.quote: Mizuhanome (彌都波能売神 or みつはのめのかみ) is a divinity of water in Japanese mythology.

claims.statement: One myth traces her birth to Izanami’s urine.
claims.statement_id: Salah satu mitos menghubungkan kelahirannya dengan air seni Izanami.
claims.quote: She was born from the urine of Izanami.

claims.statement: Atago Shrine is associated with her worship.
claims.statement_id: Kuil Atago dikaitkan dengan pemujaannya.
claims.quote: She is enshrined at Atago Shrine.

claims.statement: Other shrines dedicated to her include Ashiya and Niukawakami.
claims.statement_id: Kuil lain yang memujanya mencakup Ashiya dan Niukawakami.
claims.quote: Ashiya Shrine and Niukawakami Shrine are also dedicated to her.

claims.statement: The academic translation writes the deity’s name as Mitsuhanome.
claims.statement_id: Terjemahan akademik menulis nama dewa ini sebagai Mitsuhanome.
claims.quote: Then, from her urine a deity named Mitsuhanome no kami 弥 都 波 能 売 神 (5) came into existence.

claims.statement: Mizuhanome (Mitsuhanome) is a kami of water; when Izanami fell ill upon giving birth to the fire kami Kagutsuchi, Mitsuhanome was produced from her urine.
claims.statement_id: Mizuhanome (Mitsuhanome) adalah kami air; ketika Izanami melahirkan kami api Kagutsuchi dan jatuh sakit, Mitsuhanome muncul dari air seninya.
claims.quote: A kami of water. Upon giving birth to the fire kami Kagutsuchi, Izanami fell ill and the kami Mitsuhanome was produced from her urine.

claims.statement: According to the Nihongi, Mitsuhanome was produced just before Izanami died.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Nihongi, Mitsuhanome muncul tepat sebelum Izanami meninggal.
claims.quote: According to Nihongi, Mitsuhanome was produced just before Izanami died

claims.statement: Jinmu gave the name Itsu no Mitsuhanome ("sacred-water-female") to the water offered in the ritual by the officiating priestess Itsuhime.
claims.statement_id: Jinmu memberi nama Itsu no Mitsuhanome ("perempuan air suci") pada air yang dipersembahkan dalam ritual oleh pendeta perempuan Itsuhime.
claims.quote: Jinmu gave the name Itsu no Mitsuhanome (sacred-water-female) to the water offered as part of the ritual by the officiating priestess Itsuhime.

claims.statement: Itsu means "sacred" or "holy", mitsu (or mizu) means "water", and me is the feminine suffix.
claims.statement_id: Itsu berarti "suci", mitsu (atau mizu) berarti "air", dan me adalah akhiran feminin.
claims.quote: Itsu means "sacred" or "holy," mitsu (or mizu) means "water," and me is the feminine suffix.

claims.statement: Her name is also explained as "water snake woman" or "water dragon woman".
claims.statement_id: Namanya juga dijelaskan sebagai "perempuan ular air" atau "perempuan naga air".
claims.quote: Her name is explained as water snake woman or water dragon woman.

claims.statement: According to director Makoto Shinkai, the name of the character Mitsuha Miyamizu in the film Your Name is said to come from the goddess.
claims.statement_id: Menurut sutradara Makoto Shinkai, nama tokoh Mitsuha Miyamizu dalam film Your Name konon berasal dari dewi ini.
claims.quote: According to director Makoto Shinkai the name for the character Mitsuha Miyamizu from the movie Your Name is said to come from the goddess.

claims.statement: Mōryō is a collective term for spirits of natural places and other supernatural beings.
claims.statement_id: Mōryō adalah istilah kelompok bagi roh tempat alam dan makhluk gaib lainnya.
claims.quote: Mōryō or mizuha (魍魎, 罔両, or 美豆波) is a collective term for spirits of mountains and rivers, trees and rocks, as well as mononoke that live in places like graveyards, or kappa and various other yōkai.

claims.statement: The concept is traced to nature spirits in China.
claims.statement_id: Konsep ini dihubungkan dengan roh alam dalam tradisi Tiongkok.
claims.quote: Originally, they were a kind of spirit from nature in China.

claims.statement: The Huainanzi describes a childlike form with dark red coloring.
claims.statement_id: Huainanzi menggambarkan wujud mirip anak kecil yang berwarna merah gelap.
claims.quote: In the Huainanzi, there is the statement that "mōryō have a shape like that of a three-year-old little child, are dark red in color, have red eyes, long ears, and beautiful hair." In the Compendium of Materia Medica, there is the statement "mōryō like to eat the innards of the dead.

claims.statement: One account associates its fears with tigers and oak.
claims.statement_id: Salah satu kisah mengaitkan ketakutannya dengan harimau dan pohon ek.
claims.quote: In its true nature, the mōryō is fearful of tigers and oak, and is given the name 弗述.

claims.statement: They go underground and eat the brains of the dead, but it is said they die when an oak is pressed against their necks.
claims.statement_id: Mereka masuk ke bawah tanah dan memakan otak orang mati, tetapi dikatakan mereka mati bila kayu ek ditekan ke leher mereka.
claims.quote: They go underground and eat the brains of the dead, but it is said that when an oak is pressed against their necks, they die.

claims.statement: In Japan mōryō are sometimes regarded as the same as the kasha, the yōkai that steal corpses, and there are examples of kasha-like stories told under the name mōryō.
claims.statement_id: Di Jepang, mōryō kadang dianggap sama dengan kasha, yokai pencuri jasad orang mati, dan ada contoh cerita mirip kasha yang disebut dengan nama mōryō.
claims.quote: in Japan mōryō are sometimes seen to be the same as the yōkai that would steal corpses of the dead, the kasha, and there can be seen examples where stories similar to that of the kasha are stated under the name mōryō.

claims.statement: In the essay "Mimibukuro" by Negishi Shizumori, from the Edo period, an official named Shibata had a loyal retainer who one evening said "I'm not a human but a mōryō" and resigned.
claims.statement_id: Dalam esai "Mimibukuro" karya Negishi Shizumori pada zaman Edo, seorang pejabat bernama Shibata punya pengikut setia yang suatu malam berkata "aku bukan manusia melainkan mōryō" lalu mengundurkan diri.
claims.quote: In the essay "Mimibukuro" by Negishi Shizumori in the Edo period, a government official named Shibata had a loyal retainer, but on one evening, said "I'm not a human but a mōryō" and resigned.

claims.statement: The next day the retainer vanished, and at a funeral in the village he named dark clouds suddenly covered the place; when they cleared, the corpse is said to have vanished from the coffin.
claims.statement_id: Keesokan harinya pengikut itu lenyap, dan pada pemakaman di desa yang disebutkannya awan hitam tiba-tiba menutupi tempat itu; ketika awan menghilang, jasad dalam peti dikatakan telah lenyap.
claims.quote: The next day, the retainer disappeared, and at a funeral in the village that he mentioned, some dark clouds suddenly covered over, and when the clouds disappeared, it is said that the corpse disappeared from the coffin.

claims.statement: In Japan it is read 「みずは」, meaning a water deity, and the word is also written with various characters such as 「水波」, 「美豆波」 and 「弥都波」.
claims.statement_id: Di Jepang, kata itu dibaca 「みずは」 yang berarti dewa air, dan juga ditulis dengan berbagai aksara seperti 「水波」, 「美豆波」, dan 「弥都波」.
claims.quote: 日本では水神を意味する「みずは」と訓じ、この語は他に「水波」「美豆波」「弥都波」などさまざまな漢字で表記される。

claims.statement: According to the 『淮南子』, 罔象 arises from water, and according to the 『史記』 Confucius held that water prodigies are dragons or 罔象.
claims.statement_id: Menurut 『淮南子』, 罔象 muncul dari air, dan menurut 『史記』 Konfusius menyatakan siluman air adalah naga atau 罔象.
claims.quote: 『淮南子』によると、罔象は水から生じる。また、『史記』によると、孔子は水の怪は龍や罔象であるとした。

claims.statement: From this 魍魎 came to be regarded as a general term for water prodigies, a sense that pairs with 魑魅, prodigies of mountains and rivers (together 魑魅魍魎).
claims.statement_id: Dari situ 魍魎 pun dianggap sebutan umum siluman air, dan maknanya berpasangan dengan 魑魅, siluman gunung dan sungai (bersama-sama 魑魅魍魎).
claims.quote: これらから、魍魎も水の怪の総称とみなされるようになった。この意味は、山川の怪を意味する魑魅と対を成すようになった（あわせて魑魅魍魎）。

claims.statement: Noderabō is a yōkai in Toriyama Sekien’s illustrated collection.
claims.statement_id: Noderabō adalah yōkai dalam kumpulan gambar Toriyama Sekien.
claims.quote: The noderabō is a Japanese yōkai from Toriyama Sekien's Gazu Hyakki Yagyō and is thought to be a yōkai that appears at abandoned temples.

claims.statement: The image shows a monk-like figure beside a temple bell.
claims.statement_id: Gambarnya menampilkan sosok mirip biksu di sisi lonceng kuil.
claims.quote: The Gazu Hyakki Yagyō depicts a yōkai that looks like a monk wearing a tattered kasa standing next to a temple bell, but there is no explanation from Sekien about what this is about, so it is not known what characteristics this yōkai was intended to have.

claims.statement: Sekien did not explain the figure’s intended characteristics.
claims.statement_id: Sekien tidak menjelaskan ciri yang dimaksud pada sosok itu.
claims.quote: The Gazu Hyakki Yagyō depicts a yōkai that looks like a monk wearing a tattered kasa standing next to a temple bell, but there is no explanation from Sekien about what this is about, so it is not known what characteristics this yōkai was intended to have.

claims.statement: One later interpretation treats it as satire of monks who broke their rules.
claims.statement_id: Salah satu tafsir belakangan menganggapnya satire terhadap biksu yang melanggar aturan.
claims.quote: As it is not clear what Sekien drew here, starting from the Heisei period, several hypotheses have been put forth, and one of them supposes that this is an original creation from Sekien that was made to satirize the Edo Period monks who broke their precepts.

claims.statement: Later accounts place it in ruined temples at night.
claims.statement_id: Kisah belakangan menempatkannya di kuil terbengkalai pada malam hari.
claims.quote: They appear late at night in abandoned, overgrown, ruined temples, forlornly haunting the temple grounds and occasionally ringing the large temple bells.

claims.statement: In those accounts it sometimes rings the temple bell.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisah tersebut, ia terkadang membunyikan lonceng kuil.
claims.quote: They appear late at night in abandoned, overgrown, ruined temples, forlornly haunting the temple grounds and occasionally ringing the large temple bells.

claims.statement: A Japanese dictionary describes it as a yōkai drawn in the picture collection 画図百鬼夜行 by the Edo-period painter Toriyama Sekien: a monk in a dirty old kesa, with one view that it satirizes the precept-breaking monks of the time.
claims.statement_id: Sebuah kamus Jepang mencatatnya sebagai yōkai yang digambar dalam kumpulan gambar 画図百鬼夜行 karya Toriyama Sekien, pelukis zaman Edo; wujudnya seorang biksu berjubah tua yang kotor, dan ada pendapat bahwa gambar itu menyindir biksu pelanggar aturan pada masanya.
claims.quote: 江戸時代の画家、鳥山石燕(せきえん)の画集「画図百鬼夜行」に描かれた妖怪。汚れた古い袈裟を着た坊主の姿をしており、当時の破戒僧の風刺画との説もある。

claims.statement: One description portrays noderabō as forlorn, grotesque ghosts of fallen priests dressed in tattered rags.
claims.statement_id: Satu uraian menggambarkan noderabō sebagai hantu pendeta yang jatuh, menyedihkan dan menyeramkan, berpakaian compang-camping.
claims.quote: Noderabō are forlorn, grotesque ghosts of fallen priests dressed in tattered rags.

claims.statement: The same account says noderabō were once priests who committed some kind of sin and died in dishonor, most often by falling to vices forbidden to priests, such as attachment to women or money.
claims.statement_id: Uraian yang sama menyebut noderabō dulunya pendeta yang berbuat dosa dan meninggal dalam aib, kebanyakan karena terjerumus pada hal yang dilarang bagi pendeta seperti keterikatan pada perempuan atau uang.
claims.quote: Noderabō were once priests who committed some kind of sin and died in dishonor. Most often they are those who fell to vices forbidden to priests, such as attachment to women or money.

claims.statement: From the Shōwa period on, yōkai literature often explained the noderabō as appearing at deserted, dilapidated temples, or as the grudge of a chief priest whose temple fell into ruin for lack of villagers’ donations, appearing in the evening to ring the bell alone.
claims.statement_id: Sejak zaman Shōwa, literatur tentang yōkai sering menjelaskan bahwa noderabō muncul di kuil terbengkalai, atau berasal dari dendam seorang kepala kuil yang kuilnya merana karena kurang sumbangan warga desa, yang lalu muncul pada petang hari dan membunyikan lonceng seorang diri.
claims.quote: Beginning in the Shōwa period, literature about yōkai often explained that they are a yōkai that appear at deserted dilapidated temples or that they are resulting the grudges turned yōkai of a chief priest whose temple became dilapidated from lack of donations from villagers, which would then appear at evenings at the dilapidated temple and ring the bell alone at the deserted temple.

claims.statement: In the writings of the comic artist Mizuki Shigeru, children who heard a bell in the mountains though there was no temple were told it was the noderabō, but it was actually the mountain, a phenomenon like yamabiko.
claims.statement_id: Dalam tulisan pelukis komik Mizuki Shigeru, anak-anak yang mendengar bunyi lonceng di pegunungan padahal tidak ada kuil diberi tahu bahwa itu ulah noderabō, tetapi sebenarnya itu karena gunungnya, dengan gejala seperti yamabiko.
claims.quote: In the writings of the comic artist Mizuki Shigeru, there is a statement about the noderabō that when children would hear the sound of a bell in the mountains despite there being no temple, they were told that "it's because of the noderabō," but actually it was because of the mountain, and a phenomenon like yamabiko had occurred.

issues.message: Pernyataan hampir tidak berbagi kata dengan kutipannya sendiri. Pastikan kutipan ini benar-benar mendukung pernyataan ini (bukan kutipan milik klaim lain).

claims.statement: Onikuma is a bear yōkai from the Kiso Valley tradition.
claims.statement_id: Onikuma adalah yōkai beruang dari tradisi Lembah Kiso.
claims.quote: An onikuma (鬼熊, literally "demon bear") is a mythological Japanese yōkai originating in the Kiso Valley in Nagano Prefecture.

claims.statement: It is described as walking upright.
claims.statement_id: Ia digambarkan berjalan tegak.
claims.quote: It is a bear-like creature that has been known to walk upright.

claims.statement: Stories say it takes livestock from villages at night.
claims.statement_id: Kisah-kisah menyebut ia mencuri ternak desa pada malam hari.
claims.quote: They sneak into villages at night to carry off livestock for food.

claims.statement: It is described in the 1841 Ehon Hyaku Monogatari.
claims.statement_id: Ia digambarkan dalam Ehon Hyaku Monogatari yang terbit pada 1841.
claims.quote: It was described in the Ehon Hyaku Monogatari, a collection of supernatural tales published in 1841.

claims.statement: Accounts give it a size exceeding ordinary bears.
claims.statement_id: Kisah-kisah memberinya ukuran yang melebihi beruang biasa.
claims.quote: Onikuma continue growing and reach sizes much larger than even the largest natural bears.

claims.statement: Its dwelling is said to lie deep in the mountains.
claims.statement_id: Tempat tinggalnya konon jauh di pegunungan.
claims.quote: They live deep in the mountains, far away from humans.

claims.statement: Takuhadachijihime is a kami in Japanese mythology said to be the goddess of textiles.
claims.statement_id: Takuhadachijihime adalah kami dalam mitologi Jepang yang dikatakan sebagai dewi tekstil.
claims.quote: Takuhadachijihime (栲幡千千姫命) is a deity (kami) in Japanese mythology said to be the goddess of textiles.

claims.statement: The Kojiki identifies her as a daughter of Takamimusubi.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki menyebutnya sebagai putri Takamimusubi.
claims.quote: According to the Kojiki, she is the daughter of Takamimusubi and was married to Oshihomimi, Amaterasu's eldest son, and also gave birth to Ninigi.

claims.statement: The same account makes her the spouse of Oshihomimi and mother of Ninigi.
claims.statement_id: Kisah yang sama menyebutnya sebagai istri Oshihomimi dan ibu Ninigi.
claims.quote: According to the Kojiki, she is the daughter of Takamimusubi and was married to Oshihomimi, Amaterasu's eldest son, and also gave birth to Ninigi.

claims.statement: Yorozuhatahime is another name used in the Kojiki.
claims.statement_id: Yorozuhatahime adalah nama lain yang dipakai dalam Kojiki.
claims.quote: In the Kojiki, she is also referred to by the name Yorozuhatahime (万幡豊秋津師比売命).

claims.statement: Other names include Ame yorozu Takuhatachihatahime, Takuhatachijihime yorozuhatahime no mikoto and Honotohatahimekochijihime no mikoto (Nihongi).
claims.statement_id: Nama-nama lainnya antara lain Ame yorozu Takuhatachihatahime, Takuhatachijihime yorozuhatahime no mikoto, dan Honotohatahimekochijihime no mikoto (Nihongi).
claims.quote: Ame yorozu Takuhatachihatahime, Takuhatachijihime yorozuhatahime no mikoto, Honotohatahimekochijihime no mikoto (Nihongi).

claims.statement: She is the daughter of Takamimusuhi and, according to an "alternate writing" transmitted by the Nihongi, the younger sister of Omoikane.
claims.statement_id: Ia putri Takamimusuhi dan, menurut "tulisan alternatif" yang disampaikan Nihongi, adik perempuan Omoikane.
claims.quote: The daughter of Takamimusuhi, and according to an "alternate writing" transmitted by Nihongi, the younger sister of Omoikane.

claims.statement: She wed Amenooshihomimi no mikoto, who had been ordered to descend to the Central Land of Reed Plains; while waiting for the pacification of the Central Land she gave birth to Ninigi, who later descended in Oshihomimi's place.
claims.statement_id: Ia menikah dengan Amenooshihomimi no mikoto, yang diperintahkan turun ke Negeri Tengah Dataran Alang-alang; selagi menunggu penaklukan Negeri Tengah, ia melahirkan Ninigi, yang kemudian turun menggantikan Oshihomimi.
claims.quote: She wed Amenooshihomimi no mikoto, who had been ordered to descend to the Central Land of Reed Plains, but while waiting for the pacification of the Central Land, she gave birth to Ninigi, and he later descended in Oshihomimi's place.

claims.statement: The Kojiki and an "alternate writing" in the Nihongi also relate the birth of Hoakari no mikoto, Ninigi's elder brother and ancestor of the Owari no Muraji clan.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki dan satu "tulisan alternatif" dalam Nihongi juga menceritakan kelahiran Hoakari no mikoto, kakak Ninigi dan leluhur klan Owari no Muraji.
claims.quote: Kojiki and an "alternate writing" in Nihongi also relate the birth of Hoakari no mikoto, elder brother of Ninigi and ancestor of the clan Owari no Muraji.

claims.statement: The versions differ on the title of Ninigi's mother but agree in including elements of weaving, cloth and bountiful harvests, and in depicting Toyoakitsushihime as a link between Amaterasu, Takamimusuhi and the imperial line.
claims.statement_id: Berbagai versi berbeda soal gelar ibu Ninigi, tetapi sepakat memuat unsur tenun, kain, dan panen melimpah, serta menggambarkan Toyoakitsushihime sebagai penghubung antara Amaterasu, Takamimusuhi, dan garis kekaisaran.
claims.quote: The various versions are also inconsistent regarding the title of Ninigi's mother, but they agree in including elements relating to weaving, cloth, and bountiful harvests, and in their depictions of Toyoakitsushihime as a link between the two kami Amaterasu and Takamimusuhi, and the imperial line.

claims.statement: An alternate version says she was consort to Amenooshihone no mikoto, while another tradition says Tamayorihime, child of Yorozuhatahime, became his consort and bore Amenokihohookise no mikoto (Ninigi).
claims.statement_id: Satu versi lain menyatakan ia permaisuri Amenooshihone no mikoto, sedangkan tradisi lain menyatakan Tamayorihime, anak Yorozuhatahime, menjadi permaisuri Amenooshihone no mikoto dan melahirkan Amenokihohookise no mikoto (Ninigi).
claims.quote: An alternate version of the episode says she was the consort to Amenooshihone no mikoto, while yet another tradition states that Tamayorihime, child of Yorozuhatahime, became consort to Amenooshihone no mikoto and gave birth to Amenokihohookise no mikoto (Ninigi).

claims.statement: She is enshrined at Shiozawa Shrine in Fukushima Prefecture, Tsubaki Grand Shrine in Mie Prefecture, and Izuenashi Shrine in Osaka Prefecture.
claims.statement_id: Ia dipuja di Kuil Shiozawa di Prefektur Fukushima, Kuil Besar Tsubaki di Prefektur Mie, dan Kuil Izuenashi di Prefektur Osaka.
claims.quote: She is enshrined at Shiozawa Shrine in Fukushima Prefecture, Tsubaki Grand Shrine in Mie Prefecture, and Izuenashi Shrine in Osaka Prefecture.

claims.statement: Tarantasio is a legendary dragon associated with Lake Gerundo in Lombardy.
claims.statement_id: Tarantasio adalah naga legendaris yang dikaitkan dengan Danau Gerundo di Lombardia.
claims.quote: Tarantasio è il nome di un drago leggendario che terrorizzava gli abitanti dell'antico e ipotetico lago Gerundo (poi prosciugato, secondo la leggenda), nella zona di Lodi, in Lombardia.

claims.statement: Stories describe it as destroying boats and threatening children.
claims.statement_id: Cerita-cerita menggambarkannya merusak perahu dan mengancam anak-anak.
claims.quote: Si riteneva che questo animale mitologico divorasse i bambini, distruggesse le imbarcazioni e ammorbasse l'aria con il suo fiato pestilenziale, causando una strana malattia denominata febbre gialla.

claims.statement: Its foul breath is said to contaminate the surrounding air.
claims.statement_id: Napas busuknya konon mencemari udara sekitarnya.
claims.quote: Si riteneva che questo animale mitologico divorasse i bambini, distruggesse le imbarcazioni e ammorbasse l'aria con il suo fiato pestilenziale, causando una strana malattia denominata febbre gialla.

claims.statement: Local legends connect the dragon’s death with the lake drying up.
claims.statement_id: Legenda setempat menghubungkan kematian naga itu dengan mengeringnya danau.
claims.quote: Sono sorte poi numerose leggende riguardo al drago, tutte accomunate dalla concomitanza tra l'uccisione di Tarànto e il prosciugamento del lago.

claims.statement: According to popular legends, Lake Gerundo was inhabited by a dragon called Tarànto, more commonly known as Tarantasio, which fed above all on children.
claims.statement_id: Menurut legenda rakyat, Danau Gerundo konon dihuni seekor naga bernama Tarànto, yang lebih umum dikenal sebagai Tarantasio dan terutama memakan anak-anak.
claims.quote: Secondo le leggende popolari, il lago Gerundo sarebbe stato abitato da un dragone chiamato Tarànto, più comunemente conosciuto come Tarantasio, il quale si sarebbe nutrito soprattutto di bambini.

claims.statement: A popular tradition tells that the dragon was born from the putrefying flesh of the commander Ezzelino III da Romano, who died in those very lands.
claims.statement_id: Sebuah tradisi rakyat menceritakan bahwa naga itu lahir dari daging busuk panglima Ezzelino III da Romano, yang meninggal di wilayah itu.
claims.quote: Una tradizione popolare racconta che il drago sarebbe nato dalle carni putrefatte del condottiero Ezzelino III da Romano, morto proprio in quelle terre.

claims.statement: Some popular sources attribute the draining and reclamation of the lake to Saint Christopher, who is said to have defeated the dragon, or to Frederick Barbarossa.
claims.statement_id: Sebagian sumber rakyat mengaitkan pengeringan dan reklamasi danau itu dengan Santo Kristoforus, yang konon mengalahkan naga itu, atau dengan Federico Barbarossa.
claims.quote: Alcune fonti popolari attribuiscono il prosciugamento e la bonifica del lago a san Cristoforo, che avrebbe sconfitto il drago, o a Federico Barbarossa.

claims.statement: The most evocative version has the dragon killed by the progenitor of the Visconti, who then adopted the defeated creature, the biscione with a child in its mouth, as an emblem.
claims.statement_id: Versi yang paling memikat menyebut naga itu dibunuh oleh leluhur keluarga Visconti, yang kemudian memakai makhluk yang dikalahkan itu, yaitu ular besar dengan anak di mulutnya, sebagai lambang.
claims.quote: La più suggestiva riguarda l'uccisione del drago da parte del capostipite dei Visconti, il quale avrebbe poi adottato come simbolo la creatura sconfitta, ovvero il biscione con il bambino in bocca.

claims.statement: In fact the legend of the dragon is already spoken of in 1100 by the monk Sabbio in his memoirs on the city of Lodi.
claims.statement_id: Sebenarnya, legenda naga itu sudah dibicarakan pada tahun 1100 oleh biarawan Sabbio dalam memoarnya tentang kota Lodi.
claims.quote: In realtà, della leggenda del drago parla già nel 1100 il monaco Sabbio nelle sue memorie sulla città di Lodi

claims.statement: An explicit reference to the legend of the dragon Tarantasio is found in a fresco in the cloister of the church of San Marco in Milan, datable to the 13th-14th century, showing the mythological animal against the lake.
claims.statement_id: Rujukan eksplisit pada legenda naga Tarantasio ada dalam sebuah fresko di serambi gereja San Marco di Milan, berasal dari abad ke-13 sampai ke-14, yang menggambarkan hewan mitos itu di latar danau.
claims.quote: Un riferimento esplicito alla leggenda del drago Tarantasio si trova in un affresco del chiostro della chiesa milanese di San Marco, databile al XIII-XIV secolo, dove l'animale mitologico viene raffigurato sullo sfondo del lago.

claims.statement: A hamlet of Cassano d'Adda is named Taranta in reference to the legend.
claims.statement_id: Sebuah kelurahan di Cassano d'Adda dinamai Taranta merujuk pada legenda itu.
claims.quote: Una frazione di Cassano d'Adda è denominata Taranta in riferimento alla leggenda.

claims.statement: Some ribs of the dragon are still preserved, among others at the church of San Bassiano in Pizzighettone, Cremona; one of the ribs was studied by the naturalist Enrico Caffi in the 19th century, who identified it as belonging to a mammoth.
claims.statement_id: Konon beberapa tulang rusuk naga masih disimpan, antara lain di gereja San Bassiano di Pizzighettone, Cremona; salah satu rusuk itu diteliti naturalis Enrico Caffi pada abad ke-19, yang mengidentifikasinya sebagai milik mamut.
claims.quote: Altre costole del drago sono oggi conservate ancora invece presso la chiesa di San Bassiano a Pizzighettone, Cremona (170 cm) ... Quest'ultima costola fu studiata in particolare dal naturalista Enrico Caffi nel XIX secolo che la identificò come appartenente ad un mammuth.

claims.statement: The killing of a tarantasio dragon (which in the story denotes a species rather than a single individual) is the opening episode of the fantasy novel Donna di spade by Giuseppe Pederiali, published in 1991.
claims.statement_id: Pembunuhan seekor naga tarantasio (yang dalam kisahnya menunjuk satu spesies, bukan satu individu) menjadi episode awal novel fantasi Donna di spade karya Giuseppe Pederiali, terbit tahun 1991.
claims.quote: L'uccisione di un drago tarantasio (che nell'economia del racconto indica una specie piuttosto che un singolo individuo) rappresenta l'episodio iniziale del romanzo fantasy Donna di spade di Giuseppe Pederiali, pubblicato nel 1991.

claims.statement: According to Mentelocale, the Eni logo designed in 1952, a six-legged fire-breathing dog, was inspired by the dragon legend.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Mentelocale, logo Eni yang dirancang pada tahun 1952, seekor anjing penyembur api berkaki enam, terinspirasi legenda naga itu.
claims.quote: Luigi Broggini si ispir ... alla leggenda del drago per disegnare nel 1952 il celeberrimo logo dell’Eni: un cane sputafuoco a sei zampe.

claims.statement: Tenome is a Japanese yōkai illustrated by Toriyama Sekien.
claims.statement_id: Tenome adalah yōkai Jepang yang digambar Toriyama Sekien.
claims.quote: Tenome (手の目, eyes of hand, or rather hand eyes) is a Japanese yōkai that appeared in the Gazu Hyakki Yagyō by Toriyama Sekien.

claims.statement: It resembles a blind guildsman with eyes in the palms rather than the face.
claims.statement_id: Ia menyerupai anggota perkumpulan orang tunanetra dengan mata di telapak tangan, bukan di wajah.
claims.quote: They appear as a zatō (a kind of member of the blind persons' guild such as the tōdōza or a ranking of members of related groups such the Anma, moxibustion practitions, and members of the biwa hōshi, among other organizations) with both eyes not on the face, but on the palm of each hand.

claims.statement: Sekien’s illustration supplies no explanatory text.
claims.statement_id: Ilustrasi Sekien tidak disertai penjelasan tertulis.
claims.quote: There is no explanatory text in the Gazu Hyakki Yagyō so there are no details that can be known from it.

claims.statement: One tale places an encounter in a Kyoto graveyard.
claims.statement_id: Satu kisah menempatkan perjumpaan dengannya di pemakaman Kyoto.
claims.quote: Once, a man went on a trial of guts (or "test of courage") to the graveyard at Shichijogawara in Kyoto when a monster who appeared to be an old person around 80 years in age came after him, and this monster had eyeballs on each palm of the hand.

claims.statement: A later account describes waiting for prey to approach.
claims.statement_id: Kisah belakangan menyebut ia menunggu mangsa mendekat.
claims.quote: They wait until their prey is very close before attacking.

claims.statement: That account gives it a keen sense of smell for following victims.
claims.statement_id: Kisah itu memberinya penciuman tajam untuk mengikuti korban.
claims.quote: Tenome can run very quickly, and while their vision is not particularly strong, they have a powerful sense of smell which helps them follow their victims in the dark.

claims.statement: Waira is a yōkai pictured in Japanese scrolls and illustrated books.
claims.statement_id: Waira adalah yōkai yang digambar dalam gulungan dan buku bergambar Jepang.
claims.quote: The waira (わいら) is a Japanese yōkai from Japanese emaki (handscrolls) such as the Hyakkai Zukan by Sawaki Suushi and books such as Gazu Hyakki Yagyō (1776) by Sekien Toriyama.

claims.statement: Pictures give it an ox-like body and sharp front claws.
claims.statement_id: Gambar-gambarnya memberi tubuh mirip sapi dan cakar depan yang tajam.
claims.quote: Lee Library, Brigham Young University) it is depicted with the body of a giant ox and thick sharp claws growing on each of its front legs.

claims.statement: The old pictures do not explain its nature, and clear folk records are lacking.
claims.statement_id: Gambar lama tidak menjelaskan sifatnya, dan catatan rakyat yang jelas belum ditemukan.
claims.quote: Each of these sources have no explanatory text besides their name, and furthermore there do not exist any documents recording any folk legends about them, so it is unknown what kind of yōkai these were intending to depict.

claims.statement: Only its upper body is shown in the early pictures discussed.
claims.statement_id: Gambar awal yang dibahas hanya menampilkan bagian atas tubuhnya.
claims.quote: All of the pictures depict only the upper body, and there have been no pictures found that depict its lower half, so it is unknown what its whole body looks like.

claims.statement: A later account places it in wooded mountains near religious sites.
claims.statement_id: Kisah belakangan menempatkannya di pegunungan berhutan dekat tempat ibadah.
claims.quote: Behavior : Waira live deep in the mountains, near heavily wooded temples and shrines.

claims.statement: That account describes using its claws to catch small animals.
claims.statement_id: Kisah itu menggambarkannya memakai cakar untuk menangkap hewan kecil.
claims.quote: They also use their tough claws to dig up and catch the small animals that they feed upon, such as moles, mice, and rabbits.

issues.message: Pernyataan hampir tidak berbagi kata dengan kutipannya sendiri. Pastikan kutipan ini benar-benar mendukung pernyataan ini (bukan kutipan milik klaim lain).

claims.statement: Yamajijii is an old-man yōkai in Japanese lore.
claims.statement_id: Yamajijii adalah yōkai mirip kakek dalam kisah Jepang.
claims.quote: Yamajijii (山爺) or Yamachichi (山父) (or, depending on the area, "yamanjii") is a type of yōkai.

claims.statement: One description gives it one eye and one leg.
claims.statement_id: Satu gambaran memberinya satu mata dan satu kaki.
claims.quote: It is said to be a yōkai that takes on the appearance of an old man with one eye and one leg.

claims.statement: The tradition is documented in Shikoku, particularly Kōchi.
claims.statement_id: Tradisinya dicatat di Shikoku, khususnya Kōchi.
claims.quote: According to the Early Modern Tosa Yōkai Documentation (近世土佐妖怪資料, Kinsei Tosa Yōkai Shiryou) published by the Tosa Folkloristics Department, with the Kōchi Prefecture being the first, it was passed down in Shikoku.

claims.statement: Another description explains the apparent single eye as two eyes of very different sizes.
claims.statement_id: Gambaran lain menjelaskan kesan bermata satu sebagai dua mata yang sangat berbeda ukuran.
claims.quote: It has a height of about three to four shaku (about 90–120 centimeters) with gray hair growing all over its body and, although it has two eyes, since one of them is large and the other is unusually small, it is seen as having just one eye.

claims.statement: Accounts give its body a covering of fine gray hair.
claims.statement_id: Kisah-kisah memberi tubuhnya rambut halus berwarna kelabu.
claims.quote: Their bodies are covered in fine gray hair, and they can be found wearing old clothes, tattered rags, or nothing at all.

claims.statement: It is said to live far from settlements in the mountains.
claims.statement_id: Ia konon hidup di pegunungan jauh dari permukiman.
claims.quote: Behavior : Yamajijii live in the mountains far from human settlements.

claims.statement: Zennyo Ryūō is a rain-associated dragon deity in Japanese mythology.
claims.statement_id: Zennyo Ryūō adalah dewa naga yang berkaitan dengan hujan dalam mitologi Jepang.
claims.quote: Zennyo Ryūō (善如龍王 or 善女龍王; lit. "goodness-like dragon-king" or "goodness woman dragon-king", respectively) is a rain-god dragon in Japanese mythology.

claims.statement: According to Japanese Buddhist tradition, Kūkai made the dragon appear in 824 at the Kyoto Imperial Palace in a famous rainmaking contest.
claims.statement_id: Menurut tradisi Buddha Jepang, Kūkai memunculkan naga ini pada tahun 824 di Istana Kekaisaran Kyoto dalam lomba doa hujan yang terkenal.
claims.quote: According to Japanese Buddhist tradition, the priest Kūkai made Zennyo Ryūō appear in 824 AD during a famous rainmaking contest at the Kyoto Imperial Palace.

claims.statement: The name contains 龍王, meaning dragon king; 善 means good.
claims.statement_id: Namanya memuat 龍王, ungkapan yang berarti raja naga; 善 berarti baik.
claims.quote: The dragon name Zennyo Ryūō is written in Japanese as 善 zen "good, goodness; virtuous", 女 nyo "woman; female" or 如 nyo "like; as if; be like; thus" (differentiated with the "mouth radical" 口), and 龍王 ryūō or 竜王 "dragon king".

claims.statement: Art represents the deity as a small dragon or as a human with a dragon’s tail.
claims.statement_id: Karya seni menggambarkannya sebagai naga kecil atau manusia berekor naga.
claims.quote: Zennyo is a common theme in Japanese art, usually depicted as a small dragon but sometimes as a human, either male or female, with a dragon's tail.

claims.statement: Zennyo's best-known appearance was at the 824 Buddhist rainmaking competition at the Shinsen'en (神泉苑, "Divine Spring Garden") in Kyoto, where the priest Kūkai (Kōbō-Daishi), founder of Shingon Buddhism, and his rival Shubin (守敏) held a rain-sutra recitation contest.
claims.statement_id: Kemunculan Zennyo yang paling terkenal terjadi pada lomba doa hujan Buddhis tahun 824 di Shinsen'en (神泉苑, "Taman Mata Air Ilahi") di Kyoto, ketika pendeta Kūkai (Kōbō-Daishi), pendiri Buddhisme Shingon, dan saingannya Shubin (守敏) mengadakan lomba pembacaan sutra hujan.
claims.quote: The best-known appearance of Zennyo was during an 824 CE Buddhist rainmaking competition at the Shinsen'en or Shinzen'en 神泉苑 "Divine Spring Garden" in Kyoto. The scholar priest Kūkai or Kōbō-Daishi (774–835 CE), founder of Shingon "True Word" Buddhism, and his rival priest Shubin 守敏 held a rain-sutra recitation contest.

claims.statement: Zennyo is worshipped at the Shinto shrine Zennyo Ryūō-sha (善女竜王社) on an island in the Shinsen'en, reached by crossing the Hōsei-bashi (法成橋) bridge.
claims.statement_id: Zennyo dipuja di kuil Shinto Zennyo Ryūō-sha (善女竜王社) pada sebuah pulau di Shinsen'en, yang dicapai dengan menyeberangi Jembatan Hōsei-bashi (法成橋).
claims.quote: Zennyo is worshipped at the Zennyo Ryūō-sha 善女竜王社 Shinto shrine on an island in the Shinsen'en, reached by crossing the Hōsei-bashi 法成橋 "Dharma Completion Bridge".

claims.statement: The 835 御遺告 (Goyuigō), which records Kūkai's last words, first describes Zennyo as a golden snake eight sun (about 24 cm) long riding on the head of a dragon nine shaku (about 2.7 m) long.
claims.statement_id: 御遺告 tahun 835, yang mencatat kata-kata terakhir Kūkai, pertama kali menggambarkan Zennyo sebagai ular emas sepanjang delapan sun (sekitar 24 cm) yang menunggangi kepala naga sepanjang sembilan shaku (sekitar 2,7 m).
claims.quote: The 835 CE Goyuigō 御遺告, which records Kūkai's last words, first describes Zennyo (Fowler 1997:154) as, "a golden snake measuring eight sun 寸 (approx. 24 cm) riding on the head of a dragon measuring nine shaku 尺 (approx. 2.7 m).

claims.statement: Some versions of this Kūkai story have Zennyo coming from Mount Murō and others from Lake Anavatapta, at the center of the world in Buddhist cosmology.
claims.statement_id: Sebagian versi kisah Kūkai ini menyebut Zennyo datang dari Gunung Murō, sedangkan yang lain dari Danau Anavatapta yang berada di pusat dunia dalam kosmologi Buddhis.
claims.quote: Some versions of this Kūkai story record Zennyo coming from Mount Murō and others from Lake Anavatapta, which is at the center of the world in Buddhist cosmology.

claims.statement: Zennyo or Zentatsu (善達) supposedly lived in the Ryūketsu (龍穴, "dragon cave") on Mount Murō (室生山) in Nara Prefecture, an ancient site of dragon worship and rainmaking ceremonies in Japan.
claims.statement_id: Zennyo atau Zentatsu (善達) konon tinggal di Ryūketsu (龍穴, "gua naga") di Gunung Murō (室生山) di Prefektur Nara, tempat kuno pemujaan naga dan upacara pemanggil hujan di Jepang.
claims.quote: Zennyo or Zentatsu 善達 supposedly lived in the Ryūketsu 龍穴 "Dragon Hole/Cave" on Murōyama 室生山 "Mount Murō" in Nara Prefecture, which was an ancient locale of Japanese dragon worship and rainmaking ceremonies.

claims.statement: Kokan Shiren's Genkō Shakusho (c. 1322) has a story of the priest Keien (慶圓, 1143-1223) meeting a beautiful woman who was in fact a shapeshifting Zennyo.
claims.statement_id: Genkō Shakusho karya Kokan Shiren (sekitar 1322) memuat kisah pendeta Keien (慶圓, 1143-1223) yang bertemu seorang perempuan cantik yang sebenarnya Zennyo yang mengubah wujud.
claims.quote: Kokan Shiren's c. 1322 CE Genkō Shakusho "the Genkō era History of Buddhism" has a story about the priest Keien 慶圓 (1143–1223 CE) encountering a beautiful woman who was actually a shapeshifting Zennyo.

claims.statement: In that story the woman answers "I am the Dragon Zennyo", and the little finger she stretches out proves to be a claw more than ten shaku long that spreads a five-coloured light.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisah itu perempuan tersebut menjawab "Aku adalah Naga Zennyo", dan jari kelingkingnya yang terulur ternyata sebuah cakar lebih dari sepuluh shaku panjangnya yang memancarkan cahaya lima warna.
claims.quote: she answered: "I am the Dragon Zennyo". ... It proved to be a claw, more than ten shaku long, which spread a five-coloured light.

claims.statement: Zennyo Ryūō (善女龍王) is one of the dragon kings who are objects of rain-praying, and is also written 「善如龍王」.
claims.statement_id: Zennyo Ryūō (善女龍王) adalah salah satu raja naga yang menjadi sasaran doa meminta hujan, dan juga ditulis 「善如龍王」.
claims.quote: 善女龍王（ぜんにょりゅうおう）は雨乞いの対象である竜王のうちの一尊。「善如龍王」とも表記される。

claims.statement: On investigation, the dragon gods of the whole land had been shut in a pitcher by 守敏, who envied 空海's fame; only Zennyo Ryūō had escaped 守敏's hand, so he was summoned from the pond 無熱池 in India and is said to have sent heavy rain over the whole country.
claims.statement_id: Setelah diselidiki, dewa naga seluruh negeri ternyata dikurung dalam guci oleh 守敏 yang iri pada nama baik 空海; hanya Zennyo Ryūō yang lolos dari tangan 守敏, sehingga ia dipanggil dari kolam 無熱池 di India dan konon menurunkan hujan lebat ke seluruh negeri.
claims.quote: 調べると空海の名声を妬む守敏により国中の龍神が瓶に閉じ込められていた。しかしただ1体、善女龍王だけは守敏の手から逃れていたので天竺の無熱池（むねっち）から呼び寄せて国中に大雨を降らせたという。

claims.statement: The Zennyo Ryūō who came at 弘法 (空海)'s rain-praying is said to belong to the family of 阿那婆達多龍王, one of the Eight Dragon Kings, and to have been brought from the pond 阿耨達池 by 阿那婆達多.
claims.statement_id: Zennyo Ryūō yang datang pada doa hujan 弘法 (空海) disebut keluarga 阿那婆達多龍王, salah satu dari Delapan Raja Naga, dan dikatakan dibawa dari kolam 阿耨達池 oleh 阿那婆達多.
claims.quote: この弘法（空海）の雨乞いの際にやってきた善女龍王は、八大竜王のひとり阿那婆達多龍王の一族で、阿耨達池（あのくだっち）より阿那婆達多によって連れてこられたとされる。

claims.statement: Although it says 「善女」, its image is sometimes shown as a male deity, so it is not necessarily a goddess.
claims.statement_id: Meski disebut 「善女」, rupanya kadang digambarkan sebagai dewa laki-laki, jadi belum tentu seorang dewi.
claims.quote: 「善女」とあるが、像容は男神像で表現されることもあり女神であるとは限らない。

claims.statement: Ainu kaisei is a supernatural being in Ainu folktales.
claims.statement_id: Ainu kaisei adalah makhluk gaib dalam cerita rakyat Ainu.
claims.quote:
アイヌカイセイは、アイヌ民話に伝わる妖怪。
ぼろぼろのアットシ（シナノキやオヒョウニレの樹皮の繊維で織った、アイヌの民族衣装）を身に纏い、空家や古い家などに現れる。

claims.statement: It is described as wearing a worn attush garment.
claims.statement_id: Ia digambarkan memakai pakaian attush yang lusuh.
claims.quote: ぼろぼろのアットシ（シナノキやオヒョウニレの樹皮の繊維で織った、アイヌの民族衣装）を身に纏い、空家や古い家などに現れる。

claims.statement: Stories place it in old or empty houses.
claims.statement_id: Kisah-kisah menempatkannya di rumah tua atau kosong.
claims.quote: ぼろぼろのアットシ（シナノキやオヒョウニレの樹皮の繊維で織った、アイヌの民族衣装）を身に纏い、空家や古い家などに現れる。

claims.statement: It is said to press on a sleeper’s chest or neck.
claims.statement_id: Ia konon menekan dada atau leher orang yang tidur.
claims.quote: ぼろぼろのアットシ（シナノキやオヒョウニレの樹皮の繊維で織った、アイヌの民族衣装）を身に纏い、空家や古い家などに現れる。人が眠っていると、胸や首を押し付けて苦しめるという。

claims.statement: The folktale researcher 佐々木喜善 states in his book that there may be a connection with 座敷童子 (zashiki-warashi).
claims.statement_id: Peneliti cerita rakyat 佐々木喜善 dalam bukunya menyatakan bahwa mungkin ada kaitan dengan 座敷童子 (zashiki-warashi).
claims.quote: 民話研究家・佐々木喜善は著書において、座敷童子との関連性があるのではないかと述べている。

claims.statement: The name element 「カイセイ」 means 「死骸」 (corpse) in the Ainu language.
claims.statement_id: Bagian nama 「カイセイ」 berarti 「死骸」 (jasad) dalam bahasa Ainu.
claims.quote: 民話研究家・佐々木喜善は著書において、座敷童子との関連性があるのではないかと述べている。 なお、名称の「カイセイ」はアイヌ語で「死骸」を意味する。

claims.statement: Amatsumara is a Shinto kami associated with ironworking.
claims.statement_id: Amatsumara adalah kami Shinto yang berkaitan dengan pengolahan besi.
claims.quote: Amatsumara(天津麻羅) (“one eye of heaven”) or (ironworker of heaven) also known as “Amenomahitotsu” (Heaven's Eye One Kami) is the Shinto kami of ironworking and blacksmiths.

claims.statement: Blacksmiths regard him as a patron deity.
claims.statement_id: Pandai besi menganggapnya sebagai dewa pelindung.
claims.quote: He is also the patron kami for blacksmiths.

claims.statement: He acts as a blacksmith for the gods in Takamagahara.
claims.statement_id: Ia berperan sebagai pandai besi bagi para dewa di Takamagahara.
claims.quote: He acts as a blacksmith for the gods up in Takamagahara.

claims.statement: One story connects his work with a mirror used to bring Amaterasu from hiding.
claims.statement_id: Satu kisah menghubungkan pekerjaannya dengan cermin untuk mengeluarkan Amaterasu dari persembunyian.
claims.quote: In many versions, he made a mirror with the help of Ishikori-dome no Mikoto, which was used to lure Amaterasu from her hiding place in the rock cave of heaven.

claims.statement: The cave ritual calls for the smith Amatsumara after iron is gathered.
claims.statement_id: Ritual gua memanggil pandai besi Amatsumara setelah besi dikumpulkan.
claims.quote: iron from the Amenokanayama 天金山 mountain and sought out the smith Amatsumara 天津麻羅 (4).

claims.statement: According to the Kojiki, as the blacksmith of the Plain of High Heaven, Amatsumara was called upon to refine the iron used for making mirrors, using the "hard rocks of heaven" and the "metal mountain of heaven".
claims.statement_id: Menurut Kojiki, sebagai pandai besi di Dataran Langit Tinggi, Amatsumara dipanggil untuk menempa besi yang dipakai membuat cermin, dengan memakai "batu keras langit" dan "gunung logam langit".
claims.quote: Kojiki states that as the blacksmith of the Plain of High Heaven, Amatsumara was called upon to refine the iron used for making mirrors, using the "hard rocks of heaven" and the "metal mountain of heaven"

claims.statement: The Kogo shūi describes Amatsumara as a follower of Futodama and states that, when Amaterasu hid in the rock cave of heaven, Amenomahitotsu no kami ("the one-eyed kami of heaven") was assigned to make metal weapons.
claims.statement_id: Kogo shūi menyebut Amatsumara sebagai pengikut Futodama, dan menyebut bahwa ketika Amaterasu bersembunyi di gua batu langit, Amenomahitotsu no kami ("kami bermata satu dari langit") ditugasi membuat senjata logam.
claims.quote: Kogo shūi describes Amatsumara as a follower of Futodama; it also states that at the time of Amaterasu's hiding away in the rock cave of heaven, Amenomahitotsu no kami ("the one-eyed kami of heaven") was assigned to make metal weapons

claims.statement: The name Amatsuma(u)ra refers to the ancestral tutelary of the blacksmith occupational groups and was apparently also used as a common name.
claims.statement_id: Nama Amatsuma(u)ra merujuk pada leluhur pelindung kelompok pekerja pandai besi, dan tampaknya juga dipakai sebagai nama umum.
claims.quote: The name Amatsuma(u)ra refers to the ancestral tutelary (sojin) of the blacksmith occupational groups, and was apparently also used as a common name.

claims.statement: The name Amatsumara means ma-ura ("eye divination"), which some believe means "one-eyed", a reference to an occupational hazard of blacksmiths.
claims.statement_id: Nama Amatsumara berarti ma-ura ("ramalan lewat mata"), yang oleh sebagian orang dimaknai "bermata satu", merujuk pada risiko pekerjaan pandai besi.
claims.quote: The name Amatsumara means ma-ura ("eye divination"), which some believe means "one-eyed," a reference to an occupational hazard of blacksmiths.

claims.statement: A Japanese dictionary describes him as the smithing kami of the Kojiki who, together with Ishikoridome, made a ritual mirror to draw Amaterasu out, and who is also said to be the same kami as Amenomahitotsu.
claims.statement_id: Kamus Jepang menyebutnya kami pandai besi dalam Kojiki yang bersama Ishikoridome membuat cermin ritual untuk memancing Amaterasu keluar, dan juga disebut sebagai kami yang sama dengan Amenomahitotsu.
claims.quote: 「古事記」に見える鍛冶の神。天の岩屋戸に隠れた天照大神を導き出すため、伊斯許理度売命(いしこりどめのみこと)とともに、祭祀用の鏡を作った。天目一箇神(あめのまひとつのかみ)と同じ神ともいわれる。

claims.statement: He is discussed in the Kojiki and is associated with the giant yokai Daidarabocchi.
claims.statement_id: Ia dibahas dalam Kojiki dan dikaitkan dengan yokai raksasa Daidarabocchi.
claims.quote: He was discussed in the Kojiki and is associated to the giant yōkai Daidarabocchi.

claims.statement: Amemasu is a giant fishlike or whalelike being in Ainu folklore.
claims.statement_id: Amemasu adalah makhluk raksasa mirip ikan atau paus dalam cerita rakyat Ainu.
claims.quote: Amemasu (雨鱒（アメマス）) or Ō-amemasu (大アメマス) (rain trout) is a giant whale- or fish-like creature from Ainu folklore.

claims.statement: Accounts place large examples in lakes of Hokkaidō.
claims.statement_id: Kisah-kisah menempatkan sosok berukuran besar di danau-danau Hokkaidō.
claims.quote: Some of the largest amemasu are said to live in Lake Mashū and Lake Shikotsu in Hokkaidō, with smaller ones inhabiting lakes throughout northern areas of Honshu.

claims.statement: It is associated with overturned boats and natural disasters.
claims.statement_id: Ia dikaitkan dengan perahu terbalik dan bencana alam.
claims.quote: The amemasu are known for capsizing boats, creating earthquakes, and causing other natural disasters.

claims.statement: One story gives it a human female appearance used to lure men.
claims.statement_id: Satu cerita memberinya wujud perempuan untuk memikat pria.
claims.quote: An amemasu is able to take on a human appearance, usually of a beautiful woman, in order to lure young men to their deaths.

claims.statement: Cold, clammy skin is described as a clue to that disguise.
claims.statement_id: Kulit dingin dan lembap disebut sebagai petunjuk penyamarannya.
claims.quote: The skin of an amemasu is said to be cold and clammy, much like fish skin, which is how they can be identified when they are in human form.

claims.statement: Some accounts give it a length spanning an entire lake.
claims.statement_id: Sebagian kisah memberinya panjang yang membentang melintasi satu danau.
claims.quote: Yōkai amemasu can grow to colossal sizes, sometimes spanning an entire lake from head to tail.

claims.statement: Chōchinbi is a ghost-light type in Japanese legends.
claims.statement_id: Chōchinbi adalah jenis cahaya gaib dalam legenda Jepang.
claims.quote: Chōchinbi (提灯火) is a type of onibi, told in legends in each area of Japan.

claims.statement: It appears over footpaths between rice fields.
claims.statement_id: Ia muncul di atas jalan kecil di antara sawah.
claims.quote: It is said to appear in footpaths between rice fields, floating about one metre (3.3 ft) above the ground, disappearing when humans get close to it.

claims.statement: The light is said to disappear when people approach.
claims.statement_id: Cahaya itu konon menghilang ketika orang mendekat.
claims.quote: disappearing when humans get close to it

claims.statement: A Tokushima account describes many lights lined up together.
claims.statement_id: Satu kisah dari Tokushima menggambarkan banyak cahaya yang berbaris bersama.
claims.quote: In the Tokushima Prefecture in Shikoku, witnesses are said to have observed several tens of paper lantern fires appearing at once and lining up like light bulbs.

claims.statement: Its name comes from a resemblance to a carried paper lantern.
claims.statement_id: Namanya berasal dari kemiripannya dengan lentera kertas yang dibawa orang.
claims.quote: They appear at about the same brightness and height as a handheld paper lantern, or chōchin , which they are named after.

claims.statement: One account treats its presence as a sign of nearby yōkai.
claims.statement_id: Satu kisah menganggap kemunculannya sebagai tanda adanya yōkai di sekitar.
claims.quote: The presence of chōchinbi signals that other yōkai may be close by.

claims.statement: Its name comes from the presumption that it is some kind of monster lighting paper lanterns; it is also said to be the work of kitsune (foxes).
claims.statement_id: Namanya muncul dari dugaan bahwa ia semacam monster yang menyalakan lentera kertas; ia juga dikatakan ulah kitsune (rubah).
claims.quote: Its name comes from how it is presumed to be some kind of monster lighting up paper lanterns; it is also said to be the work of kitsune.

claims.statement: In Miyoshi District, Tokushima Prefecture, chōchinbi are called tanukibi (狸火, "tanuki fire") and are considered fires lit by tanuki.
claims.statement_id: Di Distrik Miyoshi, Prefektur Tokushima, chōchinbi disebut tanukibi (狸火, "api tanuki") dan dianggap api yang dinyalakan tanuki.
claims.quote: In Miyoshi District, Tokushima Prefecture, these chōchinbi are called "tanukibi" (狸火 , lit "tanuki fire"), and as according to their name, they are considered to be a fire lit by tanuki.

claims.statement: In Matsudzuka, Katsuraginoshimo District, Yamato Province (now Kashihara, Nara Prefecture), these mysterious fires are called koemonbi (小右衛門火).
claims.statement_id: Di Matsudzuka, Distrik Katsuraginoshimo, Provinsi Yamato (kini Kashihara, Prefektur Nara), api misterius ini disebut koemonbi (小右衛門火).
claims.quote: In Matsudzuka, Katsuraginoshimo District, Yamato Province (now Kashihara, Nara Prefecture), these mysterious fires are called koemonbi (小右衛門火 ).

claims.statement: The koemonbi appears mainly on rainy evenings on the river bank, as a mysterious fire about as big as a paper lantern.
claims.statement_id: Koemonbi terutama muncul pada malam hujan di tepi sungai, sebagai api misterius sebesar lentera kertas (paper lantern).
claims.quote: Mainly on rainy evenings, on the river bank, a mysterious fire about as big as a paper lantern would appear

claims.statement: In the tale, when Koemon struck the fire with his rod, it split into several hundred pieces and surrounded him.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisahnya, ketika Koemon memukul api itu dengan tongkat, api itu pecah menjadi beberapa ratus bagian dan mengepungnya.
claims.quote: When Koemon struck it with his rod, the fire split apart into several hundred pieces and surrounded him.

claims.statement: Koemon escaped and returned home, but that night he fell into a fever and died before he could even seek medical care.
claims.statement_id: Koemon berhasil lolos dan pulang, tetapi malam itu ia demam dan meninggal sebelum sempat berobat.
claims.quote: Koemon was surprised and was able to escape and return, but that night he fell into a fever, and without any chance to even seek medical care, he lost his life.

claims.statement: Chōchinbi often appear in long rows of dozens, one after another, resembling a string of lanterns.
claims.statement_id: Chōchinbi sering muncul dalam barisan panjang berisi puluhan cahaya, mirip untaian lentera.
claims.quote: They often appear in long rows of dozens of chōchinbi one after another, resembling a string of lanterns.

claims.statement: Chōchinbi is more or less identical to other magical fireballs; its distinguishing feature is that other spirits use it as a light source.
claims.statement_id: Chōchinbi hampir sama dengan bola api gaib lain; cirinya yang khas ialah dipakai sebagai sumber cahaya oleh roh-roh lain (used as a light source by other spirits).
claims.quote: While chōchinbi is more or less identical to other types of magical fireballs, its distinguishing feature is that it is used as a light source by other spirits.

claims.statement: In many places, chōchinbi is said to be the work of tanuki.
claims.statement_id: Di banyak tempat, chōchinbi dikatakan ulah tanuki.
claims.quote: In many places, chōchinbi is said to be the work of tanuki.

claims.statement: Fengli is a legendary flying mammal in Chinese lore.
claims.statement_id: Fengli adalah mamalia terbang legendaris dalam kisah Tiongkok.
claims.quote: Fengli (simplified Chinese: 风狸; traditional Chinese: 風狸/風貍; pinyin: fēng lí, literally 'wind leopard cat') is a legendary or mythified flying mammal of China, whose descriptions from various sources were collated in the Taiping Yulan encyclopedia (10th century) and the Bencao gangmu (16th century) compendium of materia medica.

claims.statement: Edo-period Japanese sources call it fūri.
claims.statement_id: Sumber Jepang dari zaman Edo menyebutnya fūri.
claims.quote: It is called fūri by Japanese sources dating back to the Edo period.

claims.statement: One description compares it with a small leopard-like animal.
claims.statement_id: Satu gambaran menyamakannya dengan hewan kecil mirip macan tutul.
claims.quote: The beast is described as resembling a dark-colored or blue-green (or greenish yellow and black) animal spotted like a leopard but smaller, about the size of a wildcat (leopard cat) or marten.

claims.statement: Other descriptions compare it with a monkey or rabbit.
claims.statement_id: Gambaran lain menyamakannya dengan monyet atau kelinci.
claims.quote: Alternate sources say the beast resembles a vanishingly short-tailed monkey, or a rabbit.

claims.statement: Stories give it flight or gliding among trees and rocks.
claims.statement_id: Kisah-kisah menyebut ia terbang atau meluncur di antara pohon dan batu.
claims.quote: It is capable of flying or gliding across trees or jutted rocks, eating fruits.

claims.statement: One named form is said to favor spiders as food.
claims.statement_id: Salah satu bentuk bernamanya konon menyukai laba-laba sebagai makanan.
claims.quote: Sources say that its alias fengshengshou favors eating spiders.

claims.statement: The classical Chinese text on Wikisource says the fengli, also called fengmu and fengshengshou, can leap by means of the wind, dies and revives when it catches the wind, and also treats wind ailments, which is why it has "wind" in its name.
claims.statement_id: Teks klasik Tiongkok di Wikisource menyebut fengli, juga disebut fengmu dan fengshengshou, dapat melompat dengan bantuan angin, mati lalu hidup kembali ketika terkena angin, dan juga menyembuhkan penyakit angin; karena itu ia disebut "angin".
claims.quote: 風母(《綱目》)、風生獸(同)、時珍曰..風狸能因風騰越,死則得風複生,而又治風疾,故得風名。

claims.statement: The text says the animal lives in the mountain forests of Lingnan and beyond the western frontier of Shu; it is as big as a li or an otter, looks like a small monkey with red eyes and a tail so short as to be absent, and is blue-yellow and black with markings like a leopard.
claims.statement_id: Teks itu menyebut hewan ini hidup di hutan pegunungan Lingnan dan di luar perbatasan barat Shu; ukurannya sebesar li atau berang-berang, rupanya seperti monyet kecil bermata merah berekor sangat pendek, berwarna hijau-kuning dan hitam dengan corak seperti macan tutul.
claims.quote: 其獸生嶺南及蜀西徼外山林中。其大如狸如獺,其狀如猿猴而小,其目赤,其尾短如無,其色青黃而黑,其文如豹。

claims.statement: The text says it eats spiders; by day it curls up motionless like a hedgehog, and by night it leaps very nimbly with the wind, crossing cliffs and trees like a bird flying through the air.
claims.statement_id: Teks itu menyebut ia memakan laba-laba; pada siang hari ia meringkuk tak bergerak seperti landak, dan pada malam hari ia melompat sangat lincah dengan bantuan angin, melewati tebing dan pohon seperti burung terbang di udara.
claims.quote: 其性食蜘蛛,亦啖薰陸香。晝則蜷伏不動如蝟,夜則因風騰躍甚捷,越岩過樹,如鳥飛空中。

claims.statement: The text says that if struck it dies suddenly but revives shortly afterward if its mouth faces the wind; it dies only if its bones are smashed and its brain destroyed.
claims.statement_id: Teks itu menyebut bila dipukul ia mati mendadak tetapi hidup kembali sebentar kemudian bila mulutnya menghadap angin; hanya dengan memecahkan tulangnya dan merusak otaknya ia benar-benar mati.
claims.quote: 人撾擊之,倏然死矣,以口向風,須臾複活。惟碎其骨、破其腦乃死。
