claims.statement_id: Himegami bukan nama dewa tertentu (特定の神の名前ではなく), melainkan sebutan bagi istri, putri, atau dewi yang dekat hubungannya dengan dewa utama kuil.
claims.quote: これは特定の神の名前ではなく、神社の主祭神の妻や娘、あるいは関係の深い女神を指すものである。

claims.statement: Hachiman shrines worship Hime Ōkami (比売大神); at the head shrine Usa Jingū (宇佐神宮), Ōita, and at Iwashimizu Hachimangū (石清水八幡宮), Kyoto, she is worshipped as the three Munakata goddesses (宗像三女神).
claims.statement_id: Kuil Hachiman memuja Hime Ōkami (比売大神); di Usa Jingū (宇佐神宮), Ōita, sebagai kuil induknya, dan di Iwashimizu Hachimangū (石清水八幡宮), Kyoto, ia dipuja sebagai tiga dewi Munakata (宗像三女神).
claims.quote: 八幡社では比売大神を祀る。総本宮である宇佐神宮（大分県宇佐市）や宇佐から勧請した石清水八幡宮（京都府八幡市）などでは、宗像三女神を祭神として祀る。

claims.statement: However, there are various views (諸説) on the identity of Hime Ōkami at Hachiman shrines, and it differs from region to region.
claims.statement_id: Namun, ada berbagai pendapat (諸説) tentang identitas Hime Ōkami di kuil Hachiman, dan identitas itu berbeda menurut daerah.
claims.quote: 宗像三女神を祭神として祀る。しかし、八幡社の比売大神の正体については諸説があり地域によっても異なる。

claims.statement: The Himegami worshipped at Kasuga Taisha (春日大社) is Amenomitsutamateruhime (天美津玉照比売命), wife of Amenokoyane (天児屋命); some shrines also regard Amaterasu (大日孁貴尊) as their Himegami.
claims.statement_id: Himegami yang dipuja di Kasuga Taisha (春日大社) ialah Amenomitsutamateruhime (天美津玉照比売命), istri Amenokoyane (天児屋命); ada pula kuil yang menganggap Amaterasu (大日孁貴尊) sebagai Himegami.
claims.quote: 春日大社に祀られる比売神は天児屋命（あめのこやねのみこと）の妻の天美津玉照比売命（あめのみつたまてるひめのみこと）である。大日孁貴尊（アマテラス）を比売神としている神社もある。

claims.statement: Shrines with Himegami as their main deity are found throughout Japan (日本各地); those simply called "Hime-jinja" (比売神社) are often subsidiary shrines (摂末社) of other shrines.
claims.statement_id: Kuil yang menjadikan Himegami dewa utama terdapat di berbagai tempat di Jepang (日本各地); yang hanya bernama "Hime-jinja" (比売神社) sering kali kuil cabang (摂末社) dari kuil lain.
claims.quote: 比売神を主祭神としており、日本各地にある。単純に「比売神社」と呼ばれるものは他の神社の摂末社であることが多い。

claims.statement: Hyōsube is a yōkai in Japanese folklore.
claims.statement_id: Hyōsube adalah yōkai dalam cerita rakyat Jepang.
claims.quote: Hyōsube (ひょうすべ) is a Japanese yōkai.

claims.statement: Its legends are reported in Saga and Miyazaki, among other areas.
claims.statement_id: Legendanya diceritakan di Saga dan Miyazaki serta daerah lain.
claims.quote: There are legends about them in many areas such as Saga Prefecture and Miyazaki Prefecture.

claims.statement: One description places this child-sized river being in underwater caves.
claims.statement_id: Satu gambaran menempatkan makhluk sungai seukuran anak ini di gua bawah air.
claims.quote: It is a child-sized river monster from Kyūshū that lives in underwater caves.

claims.statement: Stories associate it with nighttime activity and eating eggplant.
claims.statement_id: Kisah-kisah menghubungkannya dengan kegiatan malam dan makan terung.
claims.quote: It prefers to come out at night and loves to eat eggplants.

claims.statement: Yokai.com calls hyōsube cousins of the kappa and garappa that are more savage and belligerent.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com menyebut hyōsube sebagai sepupu kappa dan garappa yang lebih ganas dan agresif.
claims.quote: Cousins of kappa and garappa, they are more savage and belligerent.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, simply looking at a hyōsube can cause a terrible and contagious fever that can spread and turn into an epidemic.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, hanya dengan melihat hyōsube seseorang bisa terkena demam parah yang menular dan dapat berubah menjadi wabah.
claims.quote: Simply looking at a hyōsube can cause a terrible and contagious fever, which can spread and turn into an epidemic.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, hyōsube cackle with an evil laughter; a person who hears it and laughs too will be struck with fever and die within hours.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, hyōsube terkekeh jahat; orang yang mendengar dan ikut tertawa akan demam dan mati dalam beberapa jam.
claims.quote: Hyōsube cackle with an evil laughter which is also contagious; an unlucky person who hears a hyōsube laugh, and who laughs himself, will be struck with fever and die within hours.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, a hyōsube’s thick hair builds up dirt and grime, and they love nothing more than to sneak into houses at night and slip into the bathtub.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, rambut tebal hyōsube menumpuk kotoran, dan mereka paling suka menyelinap ke rumah pada malam hari lalu masuk ke bak mandi.
claims.quote: A hyōsube's thick hair builds up with dirt and grime; they love nothing more than to sneak into houses at night and slip into the bathtub.

claims.statement: Farmers living in areas inhabited by hyōsube often leave offerings of the first eggplants of the harvest in the hope that the hyōsube will spare their fields for the rest of the year.
claims.statement_id: Petani di daerah yang dihuni hyōsube sering meninggalkan terung pertama hasil panen sebagai persembahan agar hyōsube tidak mengganggu ladang mereka sepanjang sisa tahun.
claims.quote: Farmers living in areas inhabited by hyōsube often leave offerings of the first eggplants of the harvest in hopes that the hyōsube will spare their fields for the remainder of the year.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, hyōsube are occasionally honored at local Shinto shrines, usually worshiped as gods of war for some military service performed for villagers in the past.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, hyōsube kadang dihormati di kuil Shinto setempat, biasanya sebagai dewa perang karena jasa militer bagi warga desa di masa lalu.
claims.quote: Hyōsube are occasionally honored at local Shinto shrines, usually worshiped as gods of war for some military service performed for villagers in the past.

claims.statement: Yokai.com says the name is said to come from the "hyo hyo" call they make, though written in kanji the characters have a martial connotation.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com menyebut namanya konon berasal dari seruan "hyo hyo", tetapi bila ditulis dengan kanji, aksaranya bermakna kemiliteran.
claims.quote: Their name is said to come from the "hyo hyo" call that they make. However, written in kanji, the characters have a martial connotation.

claims.statement: A Japanese dictionary describes it as a yokai said to appear along mountain streams around the spring and autumn higan seasons, with lore centered on Kyushu, mainly Saga and Miyazaki, and also called Hyōsue, Hyōsubo, or Hyōsunbo.
claims.statement_id: Kamus Jepang menyebutnya yokai yang muncul di tepi sungai pegunungan pada masa higan musim semi dan gugur, dengan cerita di Kyushu terutama Saga dan Miyazaki, dan juga disebut Hyōsue, Hyōsubo, atau Hyōsunbo.
claims.quote: 日本の妖怪。山間部の渓流沿いに春秋の彼岸の時期に現れるとされる。佐賀県、宮崎県を中心とする九州地方に伝承があり、「ヒョウスエ」「ヒョウスボ」「ヒョウスンボ」などとも呼ばれる。

claims.statement: Japanese Wikipedia says one yokai illustrated guide writes that a hyōsube laughs and anyone who laughs along develops a fever and dies, but this is pointed out as probably an invention.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia bahasa Jepang menyebut satu buku bergambar yokai menulis bahwa hyōsube tertawa dan orang yang ikut tertawa akan demam dan mati, tetapi hal ini ditunjukkan kemungkinan merupakan karangan.
claims.quote: 佐藤有文『いちばんくわしい日本妖怪図鑑』には「ひょうすべが人に出遭うとヒッヒッヒッと笑い、もらい笑いした人は熱を出して死ぬ」とあるが、これは創作であろうと指摘されている。

claims.statement: Yokai.com lists the alternate names hyōsue, hyōsubo, hyōsunbo, and hyōsunbe, with a habitat of rivers and streams, found primarily on Kyushu and in West Japan.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com mencantumkan nama lain hyōsue, hyōsubo, hyōsunbo, dan hyōsunbe, dengan habitat sungai dan anak sungai, terutama di Kyushu dan Jepang bagian barat.
claims.quote: Alternate names: hyōsue, hyōsubo, hyōsunbo, hyōsunbe Habitat: rivers and streams; found primarily on Kyūshū and in West Japan

claims.statement: Ishikori-dome is a mirror-associated kami in Shinto.
claims.statement_id: Ishikori-dome adalah kami yang berkaitan dengan cermin dalam Shinto.
claims.quote: Ishikori-dome no Mikoto (石凝姥命; also 伊斯許理度売命) is a kami of mirrors in Shinto.

claims.statement: Mirror-making lineages regard this deity as an ancestor.
claims.statement_id: Klan pembuat cermin menganggap dewa ini sebagai leluhur.
claims.quote: She was regarded as an ancestral deity of Kagami zukuri no muraji (The mirror-making clans).

claims.statement: A myth gives the deity a mirror used to draw Amaterasu from her cave.
claims.statement_id: Satu mitos memberi dewa ini cermin untuk mengeluarkan Amaterasu dari guanya.
claims.quote: In Japanese mythology, she created the exquisite Yata-no-kagami mirror which lures the sun goddess Amaterasu out of her cave and returns light to the world.

claims.statement: The deity is worshiped by mirror makers and stonecutters.
claims.statement_id: Dewa ini dipuja oleh pembuat cermin dan pemahat batu.
claims.quote: Due to this achievement, Ishikori-dome is worshipped by makers of mirrors and stonecutters.

claims.statement: The Kojiki ritual assigns the making of a mirror to Ishikoridome.
claims.statement_id: Ritual dalam Kojiki menugaskan Ishikoridome membuat cermin.
claims.quote: They had the deity Ishikoridome no mikoto 伊斯許 理度売命 (5) see to the fashioning of a mirror.

claims.statement: When Amaterasu hid in the rock cave of heaven, Omoikane no mikoto had bellows made from a deer’s hide and ordered Ishikoridome to forge a mirror from metal of the mountain Amanokaguyama.
claims.statement_id: Ketika Amaterasu bersembunyi di gua batu langit, Omoikane no mikoto menyuruh dibuat pompa tiup dari kulit rusa dan memerintahkan Ishikoridome menempa cermin dari logam gunung Amanokaguyama.
claims.quote: At the time of Amaterasu's hiding away in the rock cave of heaven, the deity Omoikane no mikoto had bellows made from a deer's hide, and ordered Ishikoridome to forge a mirror from metal of the mountain Amanokaguyama.

claims.statement: The Kogo shūi states that the first mirror forged was unsatisfactory and was enshrined at the Hinokuma Jingū in Kii Province, while the second was perfect and was enshrined at the Grand Shrines of Ise (Ise Jingū).
claims.statement_id: Kogo shūi menyebut cermin pertama yang ditempa dinilai kurang memuaskan dan disemayamkan di Hinokuma Jingū di Provinsi Kii, sedangkan cermin kedua sempurna dan disemayamkan di Kuil Agung Ise (Ise Jingū).
claims.quote: Kogo shūi states that the first mirror forged at this time was unsatisfactory, and was enshrined at the Hinokuma Jingū in Kii Province. The second mirror forged was perfect and subsequently enshrined at the Grand Shrines of Ise (Ise Jingū).

claims.statement: Ishikoridome is also identified as one of the "chiefs of the five clans" who accompanied Ninigi at the Descent of the Heavenly Grandchild (tenson kōrin) and was placed in charge of forging ritual mirrors.
claims.statement_id: Ishikoridome juga disebut salah satu dari "kepala lima klan" yang menyertai Ninigi saat turun sebagai Cucu Surgawi (tenson kōrin), dan ditugasi menempa cermin ritual.
claims.quote: Also identified as one of the "chiefs of the five clans" who accompanied Ninigi at the time of the Descent of the Heavenly Grandchild (tenson kōrin), he was placed in charge of forging ritual mirrors.

claims.statement: According to the Encyclopedia of Shinto, Ishikoridome is the offspring of Amanonukato no mikoto and is claimed as ancestral deity of the Kagami-zukuri, or "mirror-maker" clan.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Encyclopedia of Shinto, Ishikoridome adalah keturunan Amanonukato no mikoto dan dianggap dewa leluhur klan Kagami-zukuri, yaitu klan "pembuat cermin".
claims.quote: Offspring of Amanonukato no mikoto, and claimed as ancestral deity of the Kagami-zukuri, or "mirror-maker" clan.

claims.statement: The Heibonsha encyclopedia says Ishikoridome made the Yata mirror to draw Amaterasu out of the rock cave and descended with the heavenly grandchild; the Nihon Shoki is also said to record that this deity made spears and bellows.
claims.statement_id: Ensiklopedia Heibonsha menyebut Ishikoridome membuat cermin Yata untuk menarik Amaterasu keluar dari gua batu dan turun menyertai cucu surgawi; Nihon Shoki juga menyebut ia membuat tombak dan pompa tiup.
claims.quote: 天照大神(あまてらすおおかみ)を岩屋戸から引き出すために八咫鏡(やたのかがみ)を作り,また天孫に随行して天下った。《日本書紀》には矛(ほこ)やふいごを作ったともある。

claims.statement: Kasuga Gongen is a collective divine identity associated with Kasuga Taisha.
claims.statement_id: Kasuga Gongen adalah identitas ilahi kolektif yang berkaitan dengan Kasuga Taisha.
claims.quote: The Kasuga Deity, also known as Kasuga Daimyojin or Kasuga Gongen, refers to both the five deities of Kasuga Taisha Shrine and a single divine entity made up of the five.

claims.statement: It refers both to five deities and to their combined divine form.
claims.statement_id: Sebutan itu merujuk pada lima dewa sekaligus wujud ilahi gabungan mereka.
claims.quote: The Kasuga Deity, also known as Kasuga Daimyojin or Kasuga Gongen, refers to both the five deities of Kasuga Taisha Shrine and a single divine entity made up of the five.

claims.statement: The group includes Takemikazuchi, Futsunushi, Ame no Koyane, Himegami and Ame no Oshikumone.
claims.statement_id: Kelompok itu mencakup Takemikazuchi, Futsunushi, Ame no Koyane, Himegami, dan Ame no Oshikumone.
claims.quote: In their separate forms, the deities are: Takemikazuchi no Mikoto, Futsunushi no Mikoto, Ame no Koyane no Mikoto, Himegami, and Ame no Oshikumone no Mikoto.

claims.statement: The deer around Nara are regarded as the deity’s messengers.
claims.statement_id: Rusa di sekitar Nara dianggap sebagai utusan dewa tersebut.
claims.quote: The deer that can be seen around Nara are considered to be the divine messengers of the Kasuga Deity.

claims.statement: The shrine’s historical account records a hall for four deities in 768.
claims.statement_id: Catatan sejarah kuil menyebut sebuah balai untuk empat dewa pada 768.
claims.quote: a shrine hall for four deities was created on November 9th in the year of 768

claims.statement: Its origin narrative connects the first deity with protecting the capital.
claims.statement_id: Kisah asal-usulnya menghubungkan dewa pertama dengan perlindungan ibu kota.
claims.quote: to the top of Mt. Mikasa in Kasuga, Nara, in order to protect the capital Heijo-kyo.

claims.statement: Kasuga-no-kami (春日神) is a Shinto deity (神道の神) also called Kasuga Myōjin (春日明神) or Kasuga Gongen (春日権現).
claims.statement_id: Kasuga-no-kami (春日神) adalah dewa Shinto (神道の神) yang juga disebut Kasuga Myōjin (春日明神) atau Kasuga Gongen (春日権現).
claims.quote: 春日神（かすがのかみ）は、神道の神である。春日明神または春日権現とも称される。

claims.statement: Shrines that worship this deity are usually named Kasuga-jinja (春日神社), and there are about 1000 of them throughout Japan (日本全国).
claims.statement_id: Kuil yang memuja dewa ini biasanya bernama Kasuga-jinja (春日神社), dan jumlahnya sekitar 1000 di seluruh Jepang (日本全国).
claims.quote: 神社の祭神を示すときに主祭神と並んで春日大神などと書かれる。春日神を祀る神社は春日神社などという社名になっており、日本全国に約1000社ある。

claims.statement: Takemikazuchi (武甕槌命, from Kashima Jingū) and Futsunushi (経津主命, from Katori Jingū) are regarded as guardian deities of the Fujiwara clan (藤原氏), while Amenokoyane (天児屋根命) and Himegami (比売神) are regarded as its ancestral deities.
claims.statement_id: Takemikazuchi (武甕槌命, dari Kashima Jingū) dan Futsunushi (経津主命, dari Katori Jingū) dianggap dewa pelindung klan Fujiwara (藤原氏), sedangkan Amenokoyane (天児屋根命) dan Himegami (比売神) dianggap leluhurnya.
claims.quote: 武甕槌命（鹿島神宮）と経津主命（香取神宮）は藤原氏（中臣氏）の守護神とされ、天児屋根命と比売神は藤原氏の祖神とされる。

claims.statement: Of the four deities of Kasuga Taisha (春日大社の四柱の神), Takemikazuchi (武甕槌命) was at first the most prominent.
claims.statement_id: Di antara empat dewa Kasuga Taisha (春日大社の四柱の神), yang pada awalnya paling menonjol adalah Takemikazuchi (武甕槌命).
claims.quote: 春日大社の四柱の神のうち、当初、特に存在感が高かったのは武甕槌命であるとされる。

claims.statement: It has been pointed out that at least until the late 11th century, when the Ōkagami (大鏡) was compiled, "Kasuga-no-kami" was still regarded as identical with Takemikazuchi (武甕槌命).
claims.statement_id: Ada pendapat bahwa setidaknya sampai paruh akhir abad ke-11, ketika Ōkagami (大鏡) disusun, "Kasuga-no-kami" masih dianggap sama dengan Takemikazuchi (武甕槌命).
claims.quote: このため、少なくとも、大鏡の成立した11世紀後半までは、「春日神」を「武甕槌命（武甕槌神）」と同一とみなす考えがあったという指摘がある。

claims.statement: Under the honji suijaku doctrine, the four kami of Kasuga Taisha are understood as local manifestations of Buddhist deities.
claims.statement_id: Menurut ajaran honji suijaku, keempat kami di Kasuga Taisha dipahami sebagai perwujudan setempat dari dewa-dewa Buddha (local manifestations of Buddhist deities).
claims.quote: The narrative is grounded in the honji suijaku doctrine, whereby the four Shinto kami enshrined at Kasuga Taisha are understood as local manifestations of Buddhist deities

claims.statement: The scroll’s tales open with an oracle of the Kasuga deity in 937, in which it calls itself Jihi Mangyō Bosatsu, "the compassionate bodhisattva of myriad deeds".
claims.statement_id: Kisah-kisah gulungan itu dibuka dengan orakel dewa Kasuga tahun 937, ketika ia menyebut dirinya Jihi Mangyō Bosatsu, "bodhisattva welas asih dengan perbuatan tak terhitung".
claims.quote: Its fifty-eight tales open with an oracle delivered by the Kasuga deity in 937, in which it identifies itself as Jihi Mangyō Bosatsu ("the compassionate bodhisattva of myriad deeds")

claims.statement: Kasuga Gongen Genki E (春日権現験記絵) is a set of painted handscrolls (emakimono) made by members of the Fujiwara clan in the early 14th century, in the Kamakura period.
claims.statement_id: Kasuga Gongen Genki E (春日権現験記絵) adalah rangkaian gulungan bergambar (emakimono) yang dibuat anggota klan Fujiwara pada awal abad ke-14, zaman Kamakura.
claims.quote: Kasuga Gongen Genki E (春日権現験記絵 ) is a set of painted handscrolls (emakimono) that was produced in the early 14th century, during the Kamakura period of Japan, by members of the Fujiwara clan.

claims.statement: The term "Gongen" means avatar or deity.
claims.statement_id: Istilah "Gongen" berarti avatar atau dewa (avatar or deity).
claims.quote: The term “Gongen” means avatar or deity

claims.statement: Kikurihime is a Shinto goddess worshiped at Shirayama Hime Shrine.
claims.statement_id: Kikurihime adalah dewi Shinto yang dipuja di Kuil Shirayama Hime.
claims.quote: Kikurihime no Kami (菊理媛神), also Kikurihime no Mikoto (菊理媛命), is a Japanese Shinto goddess venerated as Shirayama Hime (白山比咩) (also known as Shirayama Hime no Kami (しらやまひめのかみ)) at Shirayama Hime Shrine in Hakusan, Ishikawa Prefecture.

claims.statement: The Nihon Shoki mentions her, while the Kojiki does not.
claims.statement_id: Nihon Shoki menyebutnya, sedangkan Kojiki tidak.
claims.quote: She is mentioned in the Nihongi (Nihon Shoki), but not in the Kojiki.

claims.statement: One myth gives her a mediating role between Izanagi and Izanami.
claims.statement_id: Satu mitos memberinya peran penengah antara Izanagi dan Izanami.
claims.quote: She mediated between Izanagi and Izanami after the former escaped from the land of the dead, Yomi no Kuni.

claims.statement: She is also venerated at other Japanese shrines.
claims.statement_id: Ia juga dihormati di kuil-kuil Jepang lainnya.
claims.quote: She is also venerated at Yasukuni Shrine in Tokyo and at Yōrō Shrine in Gifu Prefecture.

claims.statement: According to the Encyclopedia of Shinto, at that time the kami Kukurihime is said to have mediated on behalf of Izanami, although the specific contents of her speech are not recorded.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Encyclopedia of Shinto, pada saat itu Kukurihime dikatakan menengahi demi Izanami, meskipun isi ucapannya tidak dicatat.
claims.quote: At that time, the kami Kukurihime is said to have mediated on behalf of Izanami, although the specific contents of her speech are not recorded.

claims.statement: The Encyclopedia of Shinto describes Kukurihime as a kami of mediation and negotiation.
claims.statement_id: Encyclopedia of Shinto menyebut Kukurihime sebagai kami mediasi dan negosiasi.
claims.quote: Kukurihime no kami] (Nihongi) A kami of mediation and negotiation.

claims.statement: This account is found in an "alternate writing" of the Nihongi and also in the Sendai kuji hongi, but it is omitted in the Kojiki.
claims.statement_id: Kisah ini terdapat dalam "tulisan alternatif" Nihongi dan juga dalam Sendai kuji hongi, tetapi tidak ada dalam Kojiki.
claims.quote: While this account can be found in an "alternate writing" of Nihongi and also in Sendai kuji hongi, it is omitted in Kojiki.

claims.statement: From the medieval period on, the kami came to be the central object of worship of the Shirayama Myōri Gongen shrine in Kaga Province and was generally identified with that shrine’s deity, Shirayamahime no kami.
claims.statement_id: Sejak abad pertengahan, kami ini menjadi objek pemujaan utama kuil Shirayama Myōri Gongen di Provinsi Kaga dan umumnya disamakan dengan dewa kuil itu, Shirayamahime no kami.
claims.quote: From the medieval period on, the kami came to be the central object of worship (saijin) of the Shirayama Myōri Gongen shrine in Kaga Province, and was generally identified with the deity of that shrine, Shirayamahime no kami.

claims.statement: Japanese Wikipedia says "Kukuri" in the goddess’s name is thought to mean "to bind", from her mediating between Izanagi and Izanami.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia bahasa Jepang menyebut "Kukuri" dalam nama dewi ini kemungkinan berarti "mengikat", dari perannya menengahi Izanagi dan Izanami.
claims.quote: 神名の「ククリ」は「括り」の意で、伊奘諾尊と伊弉冉尊の仲を取り持ったことからの神名と考えられる。

claims.statement: Japanese Wikipedia notes there are also views that she is Izanami’s aramitama or nigimitama, or another name for Izanami.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia bahasa Jepang mencatat ada pula pendapat bahwa ia adalah aramitama atau nigimitama Izanami, atau nama lain Izanami.
claims.quote: 伊弉冉尊の荒魂(あらみたま)もしくは和魂(にぎみたま)、あるいは伊弉冉尊(イザナミ)の別名という説もある。

claims.statement: Japanese Wikipedia says that from this tale she is regarded as having reconciled Izanagi and Izanami, and is therefore treated as a kami of matchmaking.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia bahasa Jepang menyebut bahwa dari kisah ini ia dianggap mendamaikan Izanagi dan Izanami, sehingga dipandang sebagai kami perjodohan.
claims.quote: この説話から、菊理媛神は伊奘諾尊と伊弉冉尊を仲直りさせたとして、縁結びの神とされている。

claims.statement: According to an account transmitted by the Nihongi, after the death of his wife Izanami, Izanagi went to the underworld (Yomi) to retrieve her; having broken the taboo against viewing his dead wife, he was chased back to the visible world and at the "Even Pass of the Underworld" (Yomotsuhirasaka) debated with the dead woman.
claims.statement_id: Menurut kisah dalam Nihongi, setelah istrinya Izanami wafat, Izanagi pergi ke dunia bawah (Yomi) untuk menjemputnya; ia melanggar pantangan melihat istrinya yang telah wafat, dikejar kembali ke dunia yang terlihat, dan di "Lereng Rata Dunia Bawah" (Yomotsuhirasaka) berdebat dengan perempuan yang telah wafat itu.
claims.quote: According to an account transmitted by Nihongi, following the death of his wife Izanami, Izanagi went to the underworld (Yomi) to retrieve her; breaking the taboo (kinki) against viewing his dead wife, Izanagi was chased back to the visible world, and at the "Even Pass of the Underworld" (Yomotsuhirasaka), engaged in a debate with the dead woman.

issues.message: Pernyataan hampir tidak berbagi kata dengan kutipannya sendiri. Pastikan kutipan ini benar-benar mendukung pernyataan ini (bukan kutipan milik klaim lain).

claims.statement: Kosode no te is a yōkai in illustrated books of the Edo period.
claims.statement_id: Kosode no te adalah yōkai dalam buku bergambar zaman Edo.
claims.quote: 小袖の手（こそでのて）は、鳥山石燕の妖怪画集『今昔百鬼拾遺』などの江戸時代の古書にある日本の妖怪。

claims.statement: Its image shows ghostly female hands extending from kimono sleeves.
claims.statement_id: Gambarnya menunjukkan tangan perempuan gaib yang keluar dari lengan kimono.
claims.quote: 小袖の手（こそでのて）は、鳥山石燕の妖怪画集『今昔百鬼拾遺』などの江戸時代の古書にある日本の妖怪。小袖（袖口の狭い高級な和服）の袖から、幽霊らしき女性の手が伸びたもの。

claims.statement: A later account describes attacks on clients or nearby people.
claims.statement_id: Kisah belakangan menggambarkan serangan terhadap pelanggan atau orang di sekitar.
claims.quote: This yōkai manifests as a pair of ghostly hands that emerge from the sleeves and assault welching clients—or whoever happens to be nearby.

claims.statement: That account connects the clothing with donations for funerals and prayers.
claims.statement_id: Kisah itu menghubungkan pakaian tersebut dengan sumbangan untuk pemakaman dan doa.
claims.quote: Upon death, these women’s clothes were customarily donated to a temple in exchange for a funeral and prayers.

claims.statement: An alternative in the story has the clothing sold to settle debt.
claims.statement_id: Dalam versi lain pada kisah itu, pakaian dijual untuk melunasi utang.
claims.quote: However, if the woman died still owing money to the brothel keeper, her kimono might be sold for cash instead of being donated to a temple.

claims.statement: The story explains the haunting through a spirit attached to clothing.
claims.statement_id: Kisah itu menjelaskan gangguan gaib melalui roh yang melekat pada pakaian.
claims.quote: Then, unable to properly pass on to the afterlife, her spirit might instead attach to her cherished clothing and haunt it.

claims.statement: Koto-furunushi is a musical-instrument being in Japanese supernatural lore.
claims.statement_id: Koto-furunushi adalah makhluk alat musik dalam kisah gaib Jepang.
claims.quote: The koto-furunushi (琴古主; English: "old master koto") is a fictitious being from Japanese folklore.

claims.statement: It is described as a yōkai harmless to people.
claims.statement_id: Ia digambarkan sebagai yōkai yang tidak membahayakan manusia.
claims.quote: It is a Yōkai and is said to be harmless to humans.

claims.statement: Its form resembles a koto with a demonic face.
claims.statement_id: Wujudnya menyerupai koto dengan wajah iblis.
claims.quote: The koto-furunushi has the appearance of a traditional koto (a Japanese zither), which grows a demonic face on its front.

claims.statement: The loose strings are compared with an untidy mane.
claims.statement_id: Senarnya yang tidak teratur disamakan dengan rambut kusut.
claims.quote: The strings start to meander in all directions, giving the impression of an uncombed mane.

claims.statement: One later account gives it a memory of music previously played on it.
claims.statement_id: Satu kisah belakangan memberinya ingatan tentang musik yang pernah dimainkan dengannya.
claims.quote: These yōkai may look like wild beasts, but they remember every song that was ever played on them.

claims.statement: In that account it plays music when nobody is nearby.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisah itu, ia memainkan musik ketika tidak ada orang di dekatnya.
claims.quote: Koto furunushi play when no one is around, causing everyone to wonder where the music is coming from.

claims.statement: Kubikajiri is a head-eating ghost in Japanese folklore.
claims.statement_id: Kubikajiri adalah hantu pemakan kepala dalam cerita rakyat Jepang.
claims.quote: The Kubikajiri (首かじり) is a ghost in Japanese folklore which eats the heads of its victims, be they living or dead, animal or human.

claims.statement: One account describes it as headless and accompanied by the smell of fresh blood.
claims.statement_id: Satu kisah menggambarkannya tanpa kepala dan disertai bau darah segar.
claims.quote: The creature is said to be headless itself and its presence can be distinctively detected by the smell of fresh blood.

claims.statement: That account places it in graveyards at night searching for its head.
claims.statement_id: Kisah itu menempatkannya di pemakaman pada malam hari untuk mencari kepalanya.
claims.quote: Late at night, it haunts graveyards in order to look for its own head.

claims.statement: Another description gives it long hair and sunken eyes.
claims.statement_id: Gambaran lain memberinya rambut panjang dan mata cekung.
claims.quote: They have long, disheveled hair, discolored skin, and sunken eyes.

claims.statement: That version gives it white burial clothing and no legs.
claims.statement_id: Versi itu memberinya pakaian pemakaman putih dan tubuh tanpa kaki.
claims.quote: They wear white burial robes and, like most Japanese ghosts, have no legs.

claims.statement: One explanation traces the figure to a painting by Ippitsusai Bunchō.
claims.statement_id: Satu penjelasan menghubungkan sosok ini dengan lukisan Ippitsusai Bunchō.
claims.quote: Kubikajiri developed from a painting by Ippitsusai Bunchō of a ghost eating a man’s head in a graveyard.
